Reactions to ICJ ruling underline global divisions over court with China raising concerns about judicial overreach
The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach.
Reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions. The international court of justice (ICJ) had never previously found a state responsible for genocide and the decision could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a case against Israel .
The EU hailed a “landmark” judgment from the ICJ, while the UK reaffirmed “full support” for the court and the international legal order. Australia called on Myanmar to comply fully with the judgment and its obligations under international law.
But China, which has offered rare international support for Myanmar’s military rulers since they seized power five years ago, highlighted “issues such as jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation”.
“China … believes that such practices are not conducive to the settlement of disputes,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told a news briefing when asked about the ICJ ruling. “The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue.”
Western nations cut ties with the unstable and poor south-east Asian country after the 2021 coup that ousted a civilian-led government.
Myanmar’s presidential spokesperson said on Friday that the ruling was “unfair”, noting the judges’ nine to six vote. The country’s military rulers have denied carrying out a genocide, claiming their actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted insurgent attacks.
“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” said Khaing Khaing Soe, speaking at a press conference in the capital, Naypyidaw. “So this was not a unanimous decision … I would say it is not fair.”
The US state department said on Thursday that Washington was examining the judgment, while stressing the need to avoid “politicisation” of the ICJ.
Donald Trump’s administration has taken a dim view of international law, vowing to dismantle the international criminal court (ICC), but has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.
The state department reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”, noting that the US was the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.
In Brussels, the EU said Myanmar must fully implement the ICJ’s ruling “without delay” and that “compliance with ICJ’s decisions is not optional, it is an obligation under international law”.
“The European Union holds the ICJ in the highest regard and remains steadfast in its support for its critical role in the peaceful resolution of disputes and the upholding of the rule of law at international level,” an EU spokesperson said in a statement .
“The Rohingya people have endured immense suffering, including displacement and violence, and their plight must not be forgotten. This landmark ruling underscores the imperative of justice for victims and the necessity of upholding international law.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand”.
The UK expelled Myanmar’s defence attache and called for measures to “ensure the court’s ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity”.
The ruling caps a lengthy legal campaign since August 2017 when Myanmar’s military launched what it called a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. Reports rapidly emerged of mass rapes and killings by security forces, as well as the burning of thousands of homes.
Judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.
The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the ICC – which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states – on allegations of crimes against humanity.
The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited .
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part”.
About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across the Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
Judges at the court based in The Hague have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion. An interim ICJ judgment in 2024 ordered Israel to ensure its forces do not commit acts of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia . Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

Ayasofya Camisi’nin restorasyon çalışmalarında dokuz tünel ve altı mekan bulunduğu bildirildi.
Ayasofya bilim kurulu üyesi Prof. Dr. Ahmet Güleç yapının kuzeydoğu köşesindeki hipoje (mezar yapısı) ve çevresindeki alanda yaklaşık iki yıl önce başlatılan temizlik çalışmasının sürdüğünü söyledi.
Üst örtüsünün yıkılması nedeniyle zamanla toprakla dolan alanlardaki dolgu toprak tahliye edilmiş ve kapalı alanlar ortaya çıkarılmış. Bölgede şu ana kadar altı mekan ve dokuz tünel bulundu.
Araştırması süren bazı mekan ve tünellerin Roma dönemine ait olabileceğini belirten Güleç, farklı dönemlerde de çeşitli müdahalelerle kullanılmaya devam edildiğini düşünüyor.
Son olarak iki numaralı tünelin açıldığını ve tünelde ileriye doğru çalışmaların devam ettiğini belirten Güleç, “Buradan birtakım örnekler aldık ve analizlerini yapıyoruz. Bu analizlere bağlı olarak da mekan hakkında birtakım bilgiler edineceğiz. Şu anda sadece buranın Roma dönemindeki atriumun altyapılarından biri olduğunu söyleyebiliyoruz” dedi.
Ayasofya’da en uzun tüneldeki çalışmalar 200 metreyi aştı. Eski Roma Caddesi’nin Küçük Ayasofya’dan Sarayburnu’na kadar uzandığına ilişkin tarihi kaynaklarda haritalar bulundu fakat bu güzergah henüz doğrulanmadı.
Yerebatan Sarnıcı yönüne ilerleyen tünel hattına ulaştıklarını ve ilerlemeyi durdurduklarını belirten araştırmacı, kuzey yönünde ilerledikten sonra batıya dönen başka bir tünelin de tespit edildiğini söyledi.
Sarnıcın içinden Hipodrom (At Meydanı) yönüne uzanan başka bir tünel bulunduğunu da söyleyen Güleç şöyle devam etti:
* Burada ilk açtığımız tünel, Ayasofya’ya yakın olan tünel. Güneye doğru olan tünelimiz doğrudan Yerebatan Sarnıcı’na gidiyor. Bütün bunları, içinde senelerin biriktirdiği çamurları boşalttıktan sonra takip ettik.
* Orada yaklaşık yüzde üç eğimle giden bir tünelimiz var ve hala Ayasofya’nın altından gelen suyumuz var. Muhtemelen Yerebatan Sarnıcı’na akan buradan çıkan bir kaynak ya da başka yerden gelen mesela Bozdoğan Kemeri su dağıtım şebekesinden gelen bir su olabilir ama kaynak olma ihtimali de söz konusu.
* Buranın ziyaretçiye açılması için yapılması gereken daha pek çok çalışma var. Henüz o konuda tam kesin bir karar alınmış değil.
* Bakanımız da bizler de çok istiyoruz ama burada gezdireceğimiz ziyaretçilerin sağlık, güvenlik konusu vesaire gibi birtakım bilgiler ve eylemler gerekli. Ama bu konuda gerçekten ciddi anlamda çalışmalar yapıyoruz, tartışmalarımız oluyor.

Kültür ve Turizm Bakanı Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, Ayasofya-i Kebir Cami-i Şerifi'nde devam eden kapsamlı restorasyon çalışmaları kapsamında yapının yer altındaki tünel ve mezar bölümlerinde yürütülen çalışmaları yerinde inceledi.
Ayasofya'nın tarihî tünellerine inerek çalışmalar hakkında bilgi alan Ersoy, Vezir Bahçe ve Batı Bahçe bölümlerinde yaklaşık 3 bin ton dolgu malzemesinin çıkarıldığını, toplam 420 metrelik tünel hattının temizlendiğini bildirdi.
Çalışmaların Cumhuriyet tarihinin Ayasofya'daki en kapsamlı restorasyon sürecinin bir parçası olduğunu belirten Ersoy, yer altındaki tarihî mirasın da bilimsel yöntemlerle araştırıldığını söyledi.
Ersoy'un açıklamalarında öne çıkan bulgulardan biri, Vezir Bahçe bölgesindeki hipoje olarak adlandırılan yer altı mezar yapısında ortaya çıkarılan katmanlar oldu.
Hipojedeki kazıların tamamlandığını belirten Ersoy, birbirine bağlantılı mekânlardan oluşan yapının ana bölümünün yaklaşık 8 metre uzunluğunda ve 8 metre genişliğinde olduğunu açıkladı. Yapıda doğu ve batı yönlerinde uzanan iki ayrı kanal hattı bulunduğunu kaydeden Ersoy, yaklaşık 25 metre uzunluğundaki doğu kanalının temizliğinin tamamlandığını, batı kanalındaki çalışmaların ise sürdüğünü bildirdi.
Temizlik sırasında çamurla kaplı tabanın 1,5 metre daha altına inildiğini belirten Ersoy, bu bölümün mevcut Ayasofya yapısından daha eski bir döneme ait olduğunun değerlendirildiğini söyledi.
Bakanlık, bu bulgularla yapının yer altında farklı tarihî dönemlere uzanan yapı katmanlarının da araştırıldığını belirtiyor.
Ayasofya'nın Batı Bahçe bölümünde yürütülen çalışmalarda ise altı ayrı mekân ve bunlarla bağlantılı dokuz tünel tespit edildi.
Ersoy, bu alanlardan ilk üçünün atrium olarak adlandırılan avlu yapısının bodrum katları olduğunu düşündüklerini söyledi. Üçüncü mekân üzerinden geçiş sağlanan dördüncü alanın atriumun güneyinde yer alan ayrı bir yapı olduğunu belirten Ersoy, bu bölümün batı yönünde devam ettiğini ancak bir ayırıcı duvarla bölündüğünü aktardı.
İkinci mekânın kuzey yönündeki uzantısı olan beşinci mekânın şu ana kadar 4,5 metrelik bölümünün ortaya çıkarıldığını bildiren Ersoy, bu alanın aynı doğrultuda devam ettiğinin anlaşıldığını kaydetti.
Birinci mekânın kuzeyinde ve yapıya bitişik konumdaki altıncı alanın ise Soğukçeşme Sokağı yönüne uzandığı belirtildi. Bu bölümde yaklaşık 4 metre uzunluğunda ve 4 metre genişliğinde bir alan tespit edildi.
Genişlikleri 4 ila 4,8 metre arasında değişen koridor görünümlü mekânlardan 2, 3, 5 ve 6 numaralı alanlarda çalışmalar sürüyor.
Batı Bahçe'de tespit edilen dokuz tünelden yedisinde dolgu toprağın temizliği tamamlandı. Diğer iki tünelde ise tespit ve belgeleme çalışmaları gerçekleştirildi.
Toplam 420 metre uzunluğundaki tünel hattının en uzun bölümü, 180 metreyle Tünel-4 oldu. Ersoy, bu hattın Roma Caddesi ile ilişkili olabileceğini düşündüklerini açıkladı.
Ayasofya'nın giriş cephesine paralel uzanan tünelin, Fatih Medresesi önünden başlayarak ziyaretçi giriş noktasına doğru yaklaşık yüzde 3 eğimle devam ettiği belirtildi.
Tünellerin tarih boyunca su dağıtımı ve yağmur sularının tahliyesi gibi işlevler üstlendiğini ifade eden Ersoy, çalışmaların İstanbul'un tarihî su yönetimi altyapısına ilişkin bilgileri de derinleştirdiğini söyledi.
Tünellerdeki restorasyon çalışmaları da devam ediyor. Tünel-4 ve Tünel-5'te tonozlardaki yapısal hasarların giderilmesi için 10'ar metrelik hat boyunca onarım gerçekleştirildi. Ayrıca Tünel-4'te 50 metrelik bölümün paslanmaz çelik tahkimatla güçlendirilmesi tamamlandı. Tünel-5'te ise aynı çalışma 90 metrelik hat boyunca sürdürülüyor.
Yer altındaki çalışmalar yalnızca kazı, temizlik ve belgeleme faaliyetleriyle sınırlı değil. Tarihî yapıların korunması ve güçlendirilmesi amacıyla da çeşitli müdahaleler gerçekleştiriliyor.
Bu kapsamda 56 metre uzunluğundaki Mekân-2'de, 18 metrelik hat boyunca tonozlardaki hasarlar giderildi. Onarımlarda özgün malzemeyle eş özellikte malzeme kullanıldı. Mekân-3'te ise dolgu toprağın temizlenmesi, çıkarılan malzemelerin elenmesi ve duvarlarla tonozların onarımı sürüyor.
Ersoy, yer altı bölümlerinin gelecekte ziyaretçilere açılmasına yönelik bir teşhir projesi hazırlamayı planladıklarını da duyurdu. Ancak bu sürecin yapının korunması ve ziyaretçi güvenliği esas alınarak yürütüleceğini vurguladı.
"Çalışmalarımızın bir diğer hedefi de uygun yer altı bölümlerini ziyaretçilerle buluşturmaktır. Bu doğrultuda bir teşhir projesi hazırlamayı planlıyoruz. Yapının korunmasını ve ziyaretçi güvenliğini esas alarak Ayasofya'nın yer altındaki tarihî zenginliğini de görünür hâle getireceğiz," dedi.
Çalışmalar kapsamında tünel ağının mevcut havalandırma sistemi açısından kullanılabilirliği de değerlendiriliyor.
Ersoy, mevcut yer altı tünel çıkışının yaklaşık 0,5 metrekarelik fiziki kesit alanına sahip olduğunu ve teknik değerlendirmelere göre yapının ihtiyaç duyduğu saatte 120 bin metreküplük minimum havalandırma debisinin yalnızca yüzde 3,6'sını karşılayabildiğini açıkladı.
Ana giriş kapısına yakın konumlanan mevcut menfezin, içeri verilen havanın ana mekâna yeterince dağılmadan dışarı çıkmasına neden olabileceğini belirten Ersoy, tarihî altyapının özgün işlevi ile yapının günümüzdeki mekanik havalandırma ihtiyacının ayrı ayrı ele alınması gerektiğini söyledi.
Gelecekte yapılacak lazer tarama ve belgeleme çalışmalarının ardından yer altı tünel ağının iklimlendirilmiş taze hava besleme altyapısı olarak değerlendirilmesi de gündeme gelebilecek.
Ersoy, Ayasofya'nın bütün tarihî katmanlarının korunması, bilimsel yöntemlerle belgelenmesi ve gelecek nesillere aktarılması için çalışmaların sürdürüleceğini belirtti.

A Myanmar government spokesperson said the ruling was unjust and noted that the court’s decision was not unanimous.
Myanmar’s government has rejected a ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) that its security forces conducted state-sponsored genocide against the country’s Rohingya minority, calling the judgement “unfair”.
Myanmar’s government spokesperson Khaing Khaing Soe told a news conference on Friday that the military government was a victim of injustice. China also criticised the verdict, a day after issuing a statement alongside the United States and Russia calling on international bodies such as the ICJ to refrain from abusing their jurisdiction.
The statements follow an ICJ ruling on Thursday that said Buddhist-majority Myanmar had committed genocide against its Muslim Rohingya minority in a crackdown in 2017.
“Our country was unjustly accused,” Soe said. “This ⁠⁠decision is not a ⁠⁠unanimous decision by everyone; it is not fair.”
China, which is allied to Myanmar’s military government, said that such rulings by the UN’s top court are “not conducive to the settlement of disputes”.
“The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing.
The ICJ found that Myanmar’s military carried out mass executions of men and boys, committed widespread rape and sexual violence against Rohingya women, and burned or razed hundreds of villages during so-called “clearance operations”.
Of the court’s 15 judges, nine ruled in favour of declaring genocide and six ruled against. It was the first time in the ICJ’s 80-year history that its judges had determined that a state committed genocide.
One of the court’s judges is Chinese and voted in Myanmar’s favour on all but one count.
The brutal crackdown launched by Myanmar security forces nine years ago forced about 700,000 Rohingya to seek refuge in neighbouring Bangladesh. Some also fled further afield, including to Malaysia.
The ICJ’s ruling said Myanmar had an obligation to compensate the Rohingya for the violations it had committed, to be determined later, and it must also allow the “safe and dignified return” of Rohingya displaced as a ⁠⁠result of Myanmar’s “wrongful acts”.
On Friday, Malaysia said it plans to resettle 10,000 Rohingya migrants in Turkiye as part of efforts to resolve the long-running refugee challenge it has faced.
Rohingya people make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to the United Nations.
Myanmar is in the grip of a multi-fronted civil war, including in Rakhine state where most of the country’s Rohingya lived.

The case sets a precedent for establishing a state’s intent to commit genocide beyond explicitly written orders.
After seven years of deliberations and investigations, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its minority Rohingya population.
Thursday’s ruling by the United Nations’ top court in The Hague has been viewed as historic, the first genocide verdict it has handed down since it was established in 1945.
For the majority-Muslim Rohingya – 1.2 million of whom are languishing in cramped refugee camps in Bangladesh while more than 500,000 remain trapped and targeted in Myanmar – it marked vindication and international recognition of their suffering following decades of persecution, torture and killings at the hands of the Myanmar military and non-Rohingya rebel groups in their home state of Rakhine.
This judgement has given hope to other persecuted populations around the world. It now sets a precedent to establish a government’s intent to commit genocide – a difficult aspect of such cases.
Experts say the verdict has strong implications for South Africa’s genocide case against Israel over its war on Gaza, which is one of those pending at the ICJ.
Just as Rohingya people celebrated and cried tears of joy when the court’s president pronounced a genocide ruling three hours into his readout of the verdict, many are wondering if this is a sign that Palestinians, too, will one day be able to do the same.
“This judgement will not decide the Gaza case,” Palestinian political analyst Ahmed Najar, however, told Al Jazeera. “But it may determine the legal lens through which Gaza is eventually judged.”
On December 29, 2023, three months into Israel’s war on Gaza, South Africa filed an application against Israel at the Hague court, alleging that Israel was – and is – committing genocide against the Palestinian people living there.
Pretoria requested that the ICJ first approve emergency measures to protect civilians by immediately ordering Israel to suspend its military operations.
In two days of hearings in January 2024, the ICJ ruled that it is “plausible” that Israel’s actions could amount to genocide and ordered provisional measures requesting it “take all measures” to prevent the crime, despite Israel’s arguments that it was acting in self-defence following the deadly Hamas-led attacks on army outposts and villages in southern Israel on October 7, 2023, which resulted in the deaths of about 1,200 people.
In March 2024, after South Africa had requested additional measures in light of Israel’s continued mass killings in Gaza, the court ordered Israel to ensure that food enters the enclave, finding that Palestinians in Gaza were facing famine and starvation.
In a third order in May that year, the ICJ ordered Israel to halt a deadly ground invasion in Rafah.
Israel did not comply with any of these orders, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have concluded.
At the time of the hearings in January 2024, some 23,000 people – including 10,000 children- had been killed in Gaza.
As of now, close to 75,000 people have been killed in Gaza, including an estimated 21,000 children. That does not include the thousands of people who are still missing and presumed dead under the rubble.
At least 1,662 people have been killed since an October 2025 US-brokered ceasefire agreement was announced between Israel and Hamas.
A verdict on whether Israel is committing genocide is expected to take several years as the two parties must submit written arguments and counterarguments. South Africa’s next submission will be in November 2027.
For both the Rohingya and Palestinians in Gaza, legal proceedings have offered little immediate solace: tent camps are being washed away amid intense storms for both refugee communities. Civilians are also still being killed – by continuing Israeli strikes on Gaza, most recently on the Nasser Medical Complex in southern Gaza, and by violence against Rohingya in Myanmar from both military and rebel groups.
The Gambia accused Myanmar of committing genocide against the Rohingya in November 2019.
That was two years after the Tatmadaw, Myanmar’s feared military, first began “clearance operations” that it claimed were a response to attacks on police posts by the rebel Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, which is fighting for Rohingya independence.
Myanmar denied committing crimes against civilians despite photos, videos and satellite images which showed mass killings and razed Rohingya villages, and despite gruelling accounts of torture and rape from thousands of survivors, as well as hate speech spread by senior Tatmadaw commanders.
On Thursday, nine of the ICJ’s 15-judge panel on the Rohingya case ruled that the “only reasonable inference” to be made from the evidence of widespread atrocities in Myanmar was that indeed, genocide had been committed.
The court said Myanmar had knowingly allowed civilian militias to participate in targeting Rohingya, failed to investigate or punish culpable commanders, acted with “intent” to destroy the group and prevent births, and violated provisional measures earlier issued in 2020 to preserve evidence.
“The Court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers to Bangladesh,” ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said.
It ordered that Myanmar provide reparations and restitution by ensuring the safe return of Rohingya people to their lands, replacing damaged property and compensating those affected, accounting for missing people, reuniting families and ensuring dignified burials, providing medical and trauma care, and importantly, ensuring that such violations never happen again.
Such imagery and testimonies have also been abundant in Gaza, where 2.1m people are currently concentrated in a 128sq km area (35 percent of Gaza) behind Israel’s so-called “Yellow Line”. Israel’s far-right officials have also made numerous statements debasing Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
In 2025, the Al Jazeera Investigative Unit’s feature documentary, GAZA, also exposed Israeli war crimes through the use of videos and photographs posted online by Israeli soldiers themselves.
The court’s acceptance of evidence in the Rohingya case beyond just explicit, written orders from senior military figures has led observers to conclude that it could take a similar view in relation to the war on Gaza.
United Nations expert panels have already concluded genocide has taken place in Gaza, as has the International Association of Genocide Scholars.
Like Myanmar, Israel has claimed a right to self-defence, and says it is targeting Hamas, rather than civilians, despite the majority of casualties being women and children.
In its ruling against Myanmar, the court has demonstrated that intent to commit genocide can be inferred from cumulative patterns, Najar said. “The court must assess the evidence concerning Gaza independently, but [this ruling] provides South Africa with a much clearer legal road map,” he said.
At the centre of the Myanmar case lay the central question that defined the past quarter-century: whether a state may destroy a people so long as it describes that brutality as “counterterrorism”, Anas Mustapha of the UK-based advocacy organisation, CAGE International, said.
“Today, for the first time, a court has refused to accept that defence, and Myanmar has been held to account for a genocide it carried out in that language,” he noted, adding that the US and other colonial Western nations provided the templates used against the Rohingya and Palestinians.
“The governments that wrote the language, from the invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq to the genocide in Gaza, have so far escaped any such reckoning.”
Genocide – specifically the intent to commit it – is much harder to prove than war crimes …

Posts across Facebook ‘dehumanized’ the Rohingya Muslim people, the UN’s top court has found.
In its ruling that Myanmar committed state-sponsored genocide against the Rohingya people in 2016 and 2017, the United Nations’ top court says that Facebook played a role in helping Myanmar’s military spread hate speech against its Muslim minority. The ruling from the International Court of Justice determined that Facebook posts made by the country’s military “dehumanized” the Muslim minority “and at times encouraged and legitimized violence against them,” as reported earlier by Reuters .
The decision that Myanmar committed genocide comes after The Gambia sued the country in 2019 over the military’s violent “clearance operations” targeting the Rohingya Muslims. The military relied heavily on Facebook, which was the most popular platform in Myanmar at the time of the attacks, with a 2022 report from Amnesty International finding that the platform “proactively amplified and promoted content on the Facebook platform which incited violence, hatred, and discrimination against the Rohingya.” Despite numerous warnings from human rights activists, Amnesty International said Facebook failed to stop the spread of hateful content in Myanmar.
The UN is now backing up these findings. It cites a report from the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM), which says that a post made by the military ahead of its August 25th, 2017 massacres on the Rohingya people “unleashed a torrent of public vitriol,” with over 200 comments calling for Rohingya people “to be shot, killed, exterminated or permanently removed from Myanmar.”
Facebook later removed military-linked pages containing thousands of posts with anti-Rohingya hate speech published between July and December 2017, according to the IIMM . The company admitted in 2018 that it didn’t do enough to prevent the incitement of violence in Myanmar, and later introduced a “corporate human rights policy” that includes an annual report about its impact on human rights. The Verge reached out to Meta with a request for comment but didn’t immediately hear back.

İngiltere Başbakanı Andy Burnham, AB Komisyonu Başkanı Ursula von der Leyen ve AB Konseyi Başkanı Antonio Costa, Brüksel'de düzenlenen AB-İngiltere Zirvesi'nin ardından ortak basın toplantısı düzenledi.
Burnham, Brexit referandumunun üzerinden 10 yıl geçtiğini hatırlatarak, "Bugün İngiltere için iyi bir gün, Avrupa için de iyi bir gün. Birlikte vardığımız anlaşma her iki tarafın da yararına ve İngiltere'deki kamuoyunun beklentileriyle uyumlu." diye konuştu.
İngiltere'de halkın dörtte üçünün Avrupa ile daha yakın ilişkileri desteklediğini belirten Burnham, İngiltere Hazinesinin zirvede varılan mutabakatın ülkenin Gayri Safi Yurt İçi Hasılasına (GSYH) yüzde 0,5'e kadar katkı sağlayabileceğini hesapladığını anlattı.
Burnham, yapılan anlaşmalarla İngiliz ekonomisine 17 milyar sterlinlik katkı sağlanacağını söyledi.
Yeni düzenlemelerin işletmelerin bürokrasi maliyetlerini azaltacağını ve gıda fiyatları üzerindeki baskıyı hafifleteceğini ifade eden Burnham, zirvede varılan mutabakatı uygulamaya yönelik yasa tasarısının gelecek hafta İngiltere Parlamentosuna sunulacağını anlattı.
Burnham, anlaşma kapsamındaki çeşitli politika alanlarında yapılacak değişikliklerin uygulamaya konulması için kesin tarihler belirlendiğine işaret ederek, "Eğitim ücretleri gibi çeşitli konularda ilerleyen dönemlerde ayrıca görüşmeler yapılacak. Bu İngiltere için iyi bir anlaşma. Anlaşma, ekonomimize ek bir büyüme, İngiliz halkı için yaşam maliyetlerini düşürme, işletmelerimizin üzerindeki bürokratik engelleri kaldırma ve gençlerimizin ufkunu genişletme fırsatı sunuyor." diye konuştu.
AB Komisyonu Başkanı von der Leyen de tarım ve gıda ürünleri anlaşmasının müzakerelerinin tamamlanmasının büyük bir başarı olduğunu belirterek, "Bu, Manş Denizi'nin iki yakasındaki işletmelerimiz için daha kolay ticaret ve daha düşük maliyet, tüketicilerimiz için daha fazla seçenek ve daha uygun fiyatlı gıda anlamına geliyor." değerlendirmesinde bulundu.
Karbon piyasalarını birbirine bağlayacak anlaşmanın emisyonları azaltacağını ve daha temiz sanayiye yatırımı teşvik edeceğini belirten von der Leyen, İngiltere'nin AB elektrik piyasasına katılımına yönelik çalışmaların sürdüğünü kaydetti.
Von der Leyen, İngiltere'nin 2027'de yeniden Erasmus+ eğitim programına katılacağını, müzakereleri tamamlanan gençlik programının her iki taraftan 100'er bin gence karşı tarafta 3 yıla kadar çalışma, eğitim görme, gönüllülük yapma veya seyahat etme imkanı sağlayacağını anlattı.
Von der Leyen, tarafların kritik teknolojileri ve tedarik zincirlerini korumak için ekonomik güvenlik diyaloğu kuracağını, yapay zeka ve kuantum teknolojileri gibi alanlarda dijital ortaklık başlatacağını, Manş Denizi'ndeki tehlikeli geçişleri önlemek ve göçmen kaçakçılığıyla mücadele etmek için de göç diyaloğu oluşturacağını söyledi.
Pek çok kişinin sonuçlandıramayacağını düşündüğü üç önemli anlaşmaya vardıklarını vurgulayan von der Leyen, "Bunlar, gıda ticareti, gençlerin hareketliliği ve karbon piyasasına ilişkin anlaşmalar. Üçü de önemli birer başarı. Öğrenim ücretleri ise ayrı bir konu. Önümüzdeki ay bu konu üzerinde çalışacağız. Daha önce de çözüm bulmayı başardık, bu konuda da bir çözüm bulacağımıza inanıyorum." ifadesini kullandı.
AB Konseyi Başkanı Costa, Ukrayna'ya destek ile Avrupa'nın güvenlik ve savunma ihtiyaçlarının AB-İngiltere ilişkilerinde yeni dönemin başlangıç noktası olduğunu belirtti.
İngiltere'nin AB'nin sivil kriz yönetimi misyonlarına daha düzenli katılımını sağlayacak çerçeve anlaşmanın müzakerelerinin tamamlandığını anlatan Costa, "Adil ve kalıcı bir barış sağlanana kadar Ukrayna'yı siyasi, mali ve askeri olarak desteklemeye devam edeceğiz." diye konuştu.
İngiltere'nin AB ile uzun vadeli ilişkisine dair tartışmaları ilgiyle takip ettiklerini söyleyen Costa, "İngiltere'nin AB ile uzun vadeli ilişkisinin geleceği konusunda alacağı her karara saygı duyacağız." ifadesini kullandı.
Costa, AB'nin İngiltere ile mümkün olan en yakın ilişkiye açık olduğunu belirterek, tek pazarın dört serbestisinin bölünmezliği ile hak ve yükümlülükler arasındaki dengenin bu ilişkiye yön vermeye devam edeceğini kaydetti.
Zirvenin ardından yayımlanan ortak bildiride, tarafların tarım ve gıda ürünlerinin ticaretini kolaylaştıracak anlaşmayı 1 Mart 2028'den, emisyon ticaret sistemlerini birbirine bağlayacak anlaşmayı ise 2028'den itibaren uygulamayı hedeflediği kaydedildi.
Gençlik programının sunduğu imkanların en geç Ocak 2030'da gençlerin kullanımına açılmasının amaçlandığına işaret edilen bildiride, AB ve İngiltere'nin üniversitelerinde eğitim gören öğrencilerin ödeyeceği öğrenim ücretlerine ilişkin müzakereleri zirveden sonraki 6 ay içinde tamamlamayı taahhüt ettiği belirtildi.
Bildiride, İngiltere'nin AB elektrik piyasasına katılımına yönelik müzakerelerin tarafların nihai mutabakata varması koşuluyla 2027'de sonuçlandırılması hedeflendiği, tarafların çelik ve elektrikli araç tedarik zincirlerini güçlendirmek için birlikte çalışacakları ifade edildi.
AB ile İngiltere'nin savunma kapasitesinin geliştirilmesi, askeri hareketlilik, kriz yönetimi ve deniz güvenliği alanlarında işbirliğini artıracağı belirtilen ortak bildiride, İngiltere'nin AB'nin Ortak Güvenlik ve Savunma Politikası kapsamındaki sivil misyonlarına katılımını sağlayacak çerçeve anlaşmaya ilişkin müzakerelerin tamamlandığı bildirildi.
Bildiride, İngiltere'nin AB'nin Daimi Yapılandırılmış İşbirliği (PESCO) kapsamındaki Askeri Hareketlilik ve Lojistik Merkezleri Ağı projelerine katılımına yönelik çalışmaların ilerletileceği kaydedildi.
AB ile İngiltere'nin Rusya'nın "gölge filosu" ile mücadelede bilgi paylaşımını artıracağı kaydedilen bildiride, yaptırımların delinmesini önlemek ve kritik deniz altyapısını korumak amacıyla işbirliğini güçlendireceği ifade edildi.
Ortak bildiride, Ukrayna'nın bağımsızlığı, egemenliği ve toprak bütünlüğüne desteğin yinelendiği belirtilerek, Rusya'ya saldırılarını derhal durdurması ve tam, koşulsuz ateşkesi kabul etmesi çağrısında bulunuldu.
Ukrayna'nın katılımı olmadan bu ülkede barışa ilişkin karar alınamayacağı vurgulanan bildiride, AB ile İngiltere'nin Rusya'ya yönelik yaptırımlarda eşgüdümü artıracağı ve Ukrayna'ya güvenilir güvenlik garantileri sağlanması için çalışacağı bildirildi.
Bildiride, AB'nin Ukrayna Askeri Yardım Misyonu ile İngiltere'nin Ukrayna askerlerinin eğitimine yönelik işbirliğini sürdüreceği ve İngiltere, Fransa ile Almanya'nın öncülük ettiği Gönüllüler Koalisyonu ile yakın koordinasyon içinde hareket edileceği kaydedildi.
Ortak bildiride, AB ile İngiltere'nin siber saldırılar, hibrit tehditler ve yabancı kaynaklı bilgi manipülasyonuyla mücadelede işbirliğini derinleştireceği belirtildi.

Ortak bildiride, AB ile İngiltere'nin özellikle Manş Denizi üzerinden gerçekleşen düzensiz göçü önlemek ve göçmen kaçakçılığı şebekeleriyle mücadele etmek için işbirliğini artıracağı belirtildi.
Avrupa Komisyonunun 16 Haziran 2026'da kabul ettiği Manş Denizi Eylem Planı kapsamında ortak faaliyetler yürütülmesi, sınır yönetiminin güçlendirilmesi ve ilgili kurumlar arasında bilgi paylaşımının artırılmasının kararlaştırıldığı aktarılan bildiride, tarafların düzensiz göç, üçüncü ülkelere geri dönüşler, sınır güvenliği ve yasal göç yolları konularını ele almak üzere yapılandırılmış diyalog mekanizması kuracağı bildirildi.

The US' national cyber director Sean Cairncross has been fired from his role, a source close to the White House told the AFP news agency on Thursday, following a wave of tech outages across the country.
Kirsten Davies, the defence department's chief information officer, is set to take over from Cairncross on a temporary basis, the source said.
"Congratulations to the new National Cyber Director Kirsten Davies — look forward to working together to strengthen America’s cybersecurity," US Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote in a post on social media.
At the Pentagon, Davies has acted as the "principal advisor" to Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth "on all matters relating to information management, information technology, cybersecurity, and information assurance," her bio says.
The move comes after outages have hit travel, communications and banking, as well as an internal system used by the National Security Agency in recent weeks.
The national cyber director is tasked with advising the president on cybersecurity policy and strategy, including information security and data protection as well as deterrence of "malicious" activity.
The director also coordinates cyber policy across the federal government. The office was first established in 2021.
In March, the Trump administration released a seven-page document detailing its cyber strategy.
It pledged to "act swiftly, deliberately, and proactively to disable cyber threats" by streamlining cyber regulations, modernising federal information systems, hardening critical infrastructure and maintaining an edge in AI.

White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross will be stepping down from his role, Axios reported. The news comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages whose cause remains unknown.
Cairncross, the president’s principal adviser on national cybersecurity policy and strategy, took office in August 2025. Since then, he has met with top AI leaders and helped the Trump administration make key AI decisions, according to Axios. The outlet also reports that the split between Cairncross and the White House was amicable, and his departure was timed so that the White House could nab a Senate confirmation for his role before Democrats take control of Congress in January.
Cairncross, a lawyer and longtime Republican operative, had no cybersecurity background when the Senate confirmed him 59–35. He previously served as the Republican National Committee’s chief operating officer and, during Trump’s first term, as CEO of the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a federal foreign aid agency. The office hasn’t been around long; Congress created it in early 2021, and Cairncross was only its third Senate-confirmed director. The first director, Chris Inglis, left after about 19 months, and the job then went about 10 months without a permanent director.

Sean Cairncross (left) was appointed by the Trump administration
The top cyber-security official in the US government is leaving his post after a little over a year in the job, US media report.
CBS, the BBC's US news partner, and other media report that White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross has been fired after losing the confidence of White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.
It comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors.
US officials said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks but the blackouts had sparked scrutiny from members of Congress who demanded a clearer explanation of what went wrong.
There has been no official confirmation of the removal of Cairncross but Secretary of State Marco Rubio posted on X , external to say Department of Defense chief information officer Kirsten Davies was the new national cyber director.
The AFP news agency and CBS both said sources had told them Cairncross's sacking was supported by President Donald Trump. The BBC has asked the White House for comment.
The news, first reported by Axios , external , follows security concerns, including the ability of advanced AI models - mostly from US companies - to discover vulnerabilities which humans would not be able to find on their own.
Earlier this week, Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the outages were connected, adding "we are not under systemic attack".
But the fact that so many have happened in quick succession has left some people worried about the safety of the tech which is heavily relied on in all aspects of daily life.
Hacks, AI or just overdue updates - why have there been so many outages?
Cairncross was previously a lawyer in the Republican Party, before becoming the chief operating officer of the Republican National Committee.
In the first Trump administration, he was part of the team of the White House chief of staff.
He later worked in the private sector, before returning to government in August 2025.
The White House has not publicly confirmed the departure or given a reason to why Cairncross left his role.

"Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come …but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future."
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth referred to Davies' tenure at the Pentagon as one in which "she has proven herself to be a dedicated patriot and professional."
"We are confident she will advance President Trump's America First agenda across the cybersecurity landscape," the Pentagon chief said.

Böylelikle hisse başına 83 dolar olan halka arz fiyatından toplam 1 milyar 127 milyon adet A sınıfı adi hisse senedinin ilk halka arzının tamamlandığı belirtilen açıklamada, bunun yaklaşık 1,1 milyar adedinin Anthropic tarafından ve yaklaşık 23,6 milyon adedinin belirli mevcut hissedarlar tarafından satıldığı kaydedildi.
Açıklamada, aracılık indirimleri, komisyonlar ve diğer halka arz giderleri düşülmeden önce halka arzdan elde edilen toplam brüt gelirin yaklaşık 93,5 milyar dolar olduğu ifade edildi.
Brüt gelirin yaklaşık 91,6 milyar dolarının Anthropic tarafından elde edildiği belirtilen açıklamada, şirketin mevcut hissedarlar tarafından yapılan satışlardan gelir sağlamadığı vurgulandı.
Açıklamada, halka arzın yanı sıra yaklaşık 313,3 milyon adet N sınıfı adi hissenin Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Broadcom, Google, Micron Technology, Microsoft, Nvidia ve TSMC Partners'a hisse başına 83 dolardan eş zamanlı olarak özel satış yoluyla satıldığı aktarıldı.
Bu satıştan yaklaşık 26 milyar dolar gelir elde edildiği bildirilen açıklamada, "Mevcut hissedarlar tarafından satılan hisseler de dahil olmak üzere ilk halka arz ve eş zamanlı özel satıştan elde edilen toplam brüt gelir, aracılık indirimleri, komisyonlar ve diğer halka arz giderleri düşülmeden önce yaklaşık 119,5 milyar dolar olarak gerçekleşti." ifadesine yer verildi.
Anthropic'in A Sınıfı adi hisse senetleri, dün Nasdaq borsasında "ANT" koduyla işlem görmeye başlamıştı.
Şirketin hisseleri, yüzde 34,3 primle 111,50 dolardan açılış yapmış, işlem gününü 97,17 dolar fiyatla tamamlamıştı.
Böylelikle Anthropic'in hisseleri, Nasdaq'taki ilk işlem gününde yüzde 17,1 yükselmişti.

Armed with placards and banners, demonstrators outside Anthropic’s San Francisco offices urged authorities to rein in the breakneck pace of AI development . "ASI is not a race, build it at a human pace," crowds chanted, while others called out, "What's our goal? Human control." Signs reading "Ban RSI" and "RSI - Really stupid idea" took direct aim at recursive self-improvement, the mechanism allowing AI systems to upgrade their own intelligence without human intervention.
The rally took place against a backdrop of mounting debate over AI’s impact on society, and on the heels of Anthropic’s hugely anticipated IPO , which captivated investors despite market jitters and warnings of a tech bubble. Ahead, the company faces tougher scrutiny from a Democratic-led US Congress next year , while rival OpenAI has reportedly postponed its own flotation until 2027 .
For the protesters in San Francisco, the issue went far beyond financial metrics: their demands centred on strict government regulation, public accountability and guaranteeing that human beings never relinquish control over increasingly powerful machines.

A record breaking IPO has raised billions for the AI frontier lab – but experts say the coming months could prove bumpy, as the industry faces a variety of challenges
Anthropic closes first day of public trading at $1.3tn valuation after largest-ever IPO
In the end, Anthropic’s much-anticipated IPO more than lived up to the hype. The market’s embrace of one of the AI industry’s most talked about companies has resulted in the maker of the Claude chatbot becoming one of the world’s most valuable firms after just one day of trading.
With many of the company’s founders, investors and employees now worth billions of dollars – and demand for the company’s stock remaining resilient – attention now turns to the stability of the wider market, and the global headwinds that experts say could threaten the AI industry over the coming months.
Here’s a rundown of what we can gather after a big day for Anthropic and the AI industry
Closing the day about 17% higher than its initial public offering price, Anthropic shares were trading at just over $97 when the market closed taking its valuation to roughly $1.7tn. The share price initially soared by 34% when trading got under way on Thursday, briefly taking the company’s valuation to more than $2tn.
The blockbuster debut easily places the IPO as the biggest in history , with the 980m shares sold raising $81bn, surpassing the previous record held by Elon Musk’s SpaceX’s $75bn raised in June.
Despite the excitement, major US stock indexes fells to seven-month lows on Thursday, dragged down by growing concerns about the longer-term outlook for the AI industry.
“The blockbuster Anthropic launch is a critical step in reassuring the market about the potential for AI, but ​it’s really just the beginning,” said Bob O’Donnell, chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research.
double quotation mark We still need to see ‌what happens with OpenAI, how the Nvidia situation evolves , how ‌the political climate for data centres shapes up, and what the historical performance for Anthropic proves to be before we’ll get any real sense of stability.”
In early trading on Friday, Asian stocks plunged by up to 4%, suggesting Anthropic’s debut has done little to settle nerves on trading floors.
According to reports demand for Anthropic shares was about six times what the company was able to offer, an incredible result for a company founded in 2021.
Started by a number of former OpenAI employees, Anthropic initially lagged behind its rival frontier lab, but analysts say its focus on building software for business and programming clients has helped to position it as one of the market leaders.
That breakneck growth has left investors stunned; from fledgling start-up six years ago, Anthropic is now worth more than US stock market stalwarts Walmart, JP Morgan, Visa and ExxonMobil.
The speed of its growth is reflected in its revenue: according to its investor prospectus, Anthropic brought in $16.2bn in the first six months of 2026, up from $4.6bn in revenue for all of 2025.
But Anthropic has also lost an enormous amount of money. In the first half of 2026, the company reported losses of $80bn, though that was largely due to a one-off charge. Losses grew to $104bn in the first nine months of 2026. The firm has said its costs will balloon as it invests further in datacentres.
The IPO hands Anthropic a pool of new cash to make those investments, but with promises to spend about $900bn on datacentre infrastructure over the next two decades, experts say their debt is likely to rise even further.
Newly minted Anthropic investors will also have to contend with rising public sentiment against AI.
Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei has been among the loudest voices pointing out the dangers that the products he and his rivals are developing may pose to humanity. He has called for a slowdown on the development of the most advanced AI models after employees expressed concerns that they were being built irresponsibly.
Across the US, opposition to AI companies has manifested in protests against local datacentre plans , with a number of municipalities and states voting for bans or restrictions on them at the recent midterm elections.
US economic growth is inextricably tied to the booming AI sector, and in particular the vast investments in datacentres that power programmes like Claude and ChatGPT. One estimate from Harvard professor Jason Furman suggested “investment in information processing equipment and software” accounted for 92% of the US’s GDP growth in the first half of 2025.
Any slowdown in that expenditure on datacentres could therefore have far-reaching consequences for Anthropic – and the global economy.
Anthropic’s leaders are also likely looking ahead to the changes to government next year, when Democrats take over both chambers of Congress after securing large majorities in the midterm elections.
Senior Democrats have already suggested that tech companies could face a regulatory crackdown over the dangers that advanced AI models pose, and over the volatility that AI IPOs could introduce into the economy.
Last month Democrat Elizabeth Warren, a senior member of the Senate banking committee, appeared to signal such moves, telling Amodei in a letter that Anthropic’s IPO “could inject extreme volatility and risk into the financial system, which threatens to undermine Americans’ economic security.”
double quotation mark The fact that Anthropic is burning through cash and requires an insatiable stream of capital to feed its growth is not a reason to expose everyday Americans to the company’s risks in our public stock markets … Swings in Anthropic’s share price have the potential to roil the broader markets on day one.”
Jensen Huang – the former CEO of Nvidia, the most important company in providing the advanced chips that power AI – is due to appear before Congress next month. He’ll be answering questions about his affair with a suspected Chinese spy, a scandal that has resulted in the loss of one of Silicon Valley’s key figures and sparked bipartisan national security concerns.
Earlier this year Anthropic’s chief rival, OpenAI, decided to postpone its initial offering until 2027. Experts say that Anthropic’s market reception and the movements in its share price will act as a signal to others in the industry over what the appetite for another large AI IPO will be.
Earlier this week, Open AI CEO Sam Altman said his company will go ahead with the IPO next year, even in the face of increased volatility.
Speaking to US publication Semafor, Altman appeared to take comfort from the sheer demand for Anthropic shares, leading up to Thursday’s stock market debut. “There’s been way too much investor demand and not enough supply,” he said.

Asian markets record worst week since 2020 as investors question huge sums being poured into AI build-out
Anthropic’s shares have slumped at the start of a second day of trading, as its record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies.
Shares in the frontier AI company, which floated on Thursday, fell by as much as 12% on Friday. They dropped to $85.12, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.
Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.
US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, knocking 2% off the value of the Nasdaq share index, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 10%. The broader S&P 500 share index fell 1%.
Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled -12% to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”
Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.
The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.
In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.
European stock markets were heading for their worst week since March, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.7%. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.
The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO .
Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.
“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.
Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI build out.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.
“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”
Nvidia shares fell by 3%, after California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China.
Britain’s FTSE 100 share index has dropped by 4.8% this week, and is heading for its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.
Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.
Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.
texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c680:
Anthropic's share price has dropped back towards its initial public offering (IPO) price a day after its soaring market debut, as the broader tech sell off continues.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50.
However, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping more than 10% to about $87.30, close to its IPO price of $83, and the broader stock market declines seen on Thursday continued.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index fell 2.8% in morning trade, the S&P 500 was down 1.2% while the Dow Jones Industrial Average remained largely flat.
The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading.
The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.
Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."
Nvidia and SpaceX were both down more than 6%, while Tesla shares fell more than 3% and Meta was down 3.4%.
Apple, Amazon and Microsoft experienced smaller falls, while Alphabet was up by 1.2%.
Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - were also trading lower. Germany's Dax index fell 2% and the UK's FTSE 100 was down 0.5%.
Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.
South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.
Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

News of operation comes after supermarkets in at least seven European countries hit by cyber-attacks
A secret government cybersecurity operation recently thwarted a cyber-attack on fridges and freezers in UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums, it has emerged.
The attack would have been similar to those that have caused many millions of euros of damage in continental Europe in recent months. But, while many retailers have now been protected, researchers warned that many more could still be vulnerable.
News of the operation led by Whitehall and the National Cyber Security Centre, first reported by the BBC, comes after supermarket chains in at least seven European countries were affected by a cyber-attack this month.
Another wave of attacks also affected hundreds of retailers across France in October in an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression” for which Paris has publicly blamed Iran . The Pentagon is also investigating a suspected hack after a series of fridge malfunctions hit at least six US military bases in August.
Experts told the Guardian that, if the vulnerability in UK-based devices had been discovered and exploited before a fix was found, the consequences would have been serious.
“This incident should serve as a wake-up call for the entire refrigeration industry,” said Garry Turner-Smith of Omega Solutions, a refrigeration consultancy firm whose employee, Neil McCourt, found the vulnerability in devices manufactured by Resource Data Management (RDM).
“Had these weaknesses been discovered and exploited by someone with malicious intentions, they could potentially have gained full control of vulnerable RDM data managers and used that access to interfere with refrigeration systems across multiple sites. This raises the prospect of attacks similar to those seen in Europe,” he said.
After Omega was alerted to the weakness, the firm called in the cyber-security consultants Pen Test Partners to investigate. Both firms then raised their concerns with the manufacturer, RDM.
“We determined that there was an urgent requirement to alert supermarkets and the food supply chain to the issue and fix,” said Pen Test Partners’ managing partner, Ken Munro. “However, we also had to work quietly to avoid alerting less ethical hackers and nation states of the likes of Iran, who are active in this space.”
Munro was fortunately attending a retail industry cyber event the day the vulnerabilities were found, enabling him to meet National Cyber Security Centre representatives in person to share the intelligence.
That triggered a series of briefing calls between retailers and officials from the National Cyber Security Centre, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs and the Food Standards Agency, among others, Munro said.
He added that Pen Test Partners also tried to alert the owners of exposed devices. “Some controllers were easy to identify and thus contact the owners, but many thousands at small stores are still exposed,” he said.
“The vulnerability is not easy to find for a number of reasons, but once the method is known, it’s easy to recreate. We have not published that method, so there is still time for small operators to take their controllers off the public internet and/or apply the updated firmware.”
A National Cyber Security Centre spokesperson said it “shared important insight and security advice to ensure that organisations understood potential risks to their networks, and were taking the appropriate measures to mitigate them”.
RDM did not respond to a request for comment. Its chief executive, Ged Evans, told the BBC the vulnerability was “identified in a test environment” that “went beyond” what such exercises usually involved, as it “included dismantling our hardware”.
“In any event we have acted at pace to address this issue and have already deployed first patch releases and have been in proactive contact with our customers to flag any issues and recommend mitigatory steps,” he said.
texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6eq:
Sweden was among countries to report a cyber incident in which some supermarket fridge units had been hiked up in temperature
A behind the scenes cyber-security operation has taken place to secure tens of thousands of fridges and freezers at major UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums from hackers, the BBC has learned.
Recent waves of cyber-attacks in Europe have seen tonnes of food spoiled at hundreds of stores, causing millions of pounds of damage.
France has blamed Iran for one of the waves of attacks that impacted its supermarkets, a claim Tehran denies .
It was thought the UK had largely escaped such hacks as the British refrigeration industry relies on different devices but there was in fact a potential vulnerability the sector has been rushing to fix.
In late October, security researchers discovered a major flaw that, if found by hackers, could have led to even worse damage to the UK.
Since then, researchers, IT teams and the National Cyber Security Centre have been working around the clock to warn dozens of companies.
The BBC has not reported on the large-scale, secretive operation until now to reduce the chances of hackers causing harm if they found the vulnerability.
As Europe sees a wave of cyber-attacks on commercial fridges, we investigate how everyday devices are vulnerable to basic attacks using easily-available tools.
The security threat was discovered by staff at refrigeration consultants Omega Solutions - it was then verified and expanded upon by experts at Pen Test Partners who helped raise the alarm.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) were then involved in the campaign to plug the security holes.
They held industry conference calls and tasked teams to contact firms at risk.
Thousands of devices controlling tens of thousands of refrigeration devices were taken off the open internet either remotely or, in some cases, physically - with staff ordered to remove internet cables and monitor temperatures manually.
BBC news has learnt most major supermarkets have been forced to divert IT teams to address the risks, with a worker at one large chain saying they took hundreds of devices offline every day over the course of a week.
"It did feel like a race against time as we were expecting another wave of these fridge hacks to come," said the person, who did not want to be publicly named.
"From a business perspective it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems. Our warehouses have millions of pounds worth of food that could have been spoiled if any hackers found out about this method of attack," they added.
There have been three waves of hacks on refrigeration temperature controllers so far this year:
In August, fridges at a small number of US military bases were impacted
On 11 and 12 October hundreds of supermarkets and food processing sites in France were hit when Danfoss temperature control systems were targeted
On 1 and 2 November dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries were hit, with Belgium and Luxembourg the worst affected. A small number of blood bank sites in France were also impacted
The waves of attacks prompted an expert at Omega Solutions to examine the security of the most popular refrigeration controllers in the UK, made by British firm Resource Data Management (RDM).
RDM disputes the critical nature of the vulnerabilities exposed but has been praised for its professional response to address the concerns, the BBC understands.
As well as supermarkets, multiple other areas of UK food and beverage industry were also warned to take action about the risks.
These include convenience stores, petrol stations, restaurants and fast food chains, sports arenas, hotels, food processing plants and cold storage sites.
Each RDM controller can be used to remotely control the temperature of dozens of fridges and freezers
"These popular controllers had a similar weak password problem to the Danfoss and other controllers that were attacked so successfully in previous hacks so we had to get the message out as soon as possible and keep it secret," said Ken Munro of Pen Test Partners.
"There is so much extra attention on these ubiquitous bits of kit now that it was likely a matter of days until criminals or nation state hackers figured it out," he added.
RDM, though, says comparisons with the units attacked in mainland Europe are not fair because hacking their fridges and freezers would have involved getting hold of a piece of hardware.
The ethical hackers say this would have been achievable as the hardware in question can be purchased cheaply online on sites like eBay.
"This was a vulnerability identified in a test environment," said Ged Evans, CEO of RDM.
He said the test "went beyond" what such exercises usually involved, as it "included dismantling our hardware".
"In any event we have acted at pace to address this issue and have already deployed first patch releases and have been in proactive contact with our customers to flag any issues and recommend mitigatory steps," he added.
RDM confirmed that there was no sign of any malicious activity on the controllers and that it continued to work with the NCSC and other authorities to monitor the situation.

texts.https://www.bloomberght.com/anthropic-hi:
Rekor tutarla halka arz edilen yapay zeka şirketi Anthropic 'te ikinci günde de satışların devam ettiği görülüyor.
Şirketin hisseleri halka arzın ikinci gününde piyasa öncesi satışlarda yüzde 14'e varan gerileme kaydetti.
Anthropic hisseleri, şirketin 107,3 milyar dolarlık rekor halka arzının ardından ilk işlem gününde yüzde 17 oranında yükseliş kaydettikten sonra, kapanış sonrası işlemlerde yaklaşık yüzde 5 düşmüştü.
Claude sohbet robotunun geliştiricisinin güçlü açılışı, yoğun talep gören halka arzın ardından yatırımcıların şirkete yönelik büyük iştahını yansıtsa da yüksek değerleme ve yeni rekabet tehditleri kapanış sonrası işlemlerde hisse üzerinde baskı yarattı ve bu ivmenin ne kadar sürdürülebileceğine ilişkin endişeleri artırdı.
Singapur merkezli Reed Capital’ın yatırım direktörü Gerald Gan, “Yapay zeka rallisini destekleyen son sütun da çöküyor gibi görünürken piyasa algısı artık oldukça kötümser” dedi. Gan, daha cazip değerlemelerden kaliteli hisseler toplamaya hazırlandığını ancak düşen piyasada çok erken alım yapma riskinin de farkında olduğunu söyledi.
Tandem Investment Advisors yatırım direktörü Jordan Watson, “Yapay zekaya yönelik algının kötüleşmeye devam ettiğini görüyoruz. Anthropic şu anda yapay zeka risk iştahının en şeffaf ve gerçek zamanlı göstergesi” dedi.
Union Bancaire Privee Genel Müdürü Vey-Sern Ling, “İlk gün diğer halka arzlarda olduğu gibi güçlü bir yükseliş yaşandı ancak yapay zeka yatırım temasındaki kötümserliği dağıtmak için önümüzdeki çeyreklerde güçlü sonuçlar, yapay zeka için yeni kullanım alanları ve gelir yaratmanın hızlandığını görmemiz gerekecek” dedi.
Goldman Sachs analistleri şirketin yıllık bazda pozitif serbest nakit akışına ulaşmasının 2030’u bulmasını bekliyor. Analistler, buna karşılık Anthropic’in yıllık gelirinin 2030’a kadar yaklaşık 685 milyar dolara ulaşacağını tahmin ediyorlar.
texts.https://www.bloomberght.com/appledan-ope:
Apple , kullanıcılar adına görevleri yerine getirebilecek kendi otonom yapay zeka ajanını geliştirerek OpenAI , Anthropic , Meta ve diğer şirketlerin faaliyet gösterdiği hızla büyüyen pazara girmeye hazırlanıyor.
Şirket planlarını bu hafta internet sitesinde yayımladığı iş ilanları vasıtasıyla açıkladı. İlanlardan birinde Apple, proaktif bir yapay zeka asistanı için kıdemli mühendislik yöneticisi aradığını belirtti. İlanda sistemin kullanıcı adına kod yazabileceği, internette gezinebileceği, uygulamaları kontrol edebileceği ve cihazlarda işlem yapabileceği belirtildi.
Apple’ın hamlesi, Meta’nın Muse adlı aracının restoran rezervasyonu yapma, seyahat planlama ve haber özetleri hazırlama gibi özellikleriyle son aylarda tüketicilerin ilgisini çekmesinin ardından geldi. Yapay zekanın Mac bilgisayarları kontrol etmesini ve yazılım geliştirmesini sağlayan araçların sayısı da hızla artıyor.
Anthropic kısa süre önce Duet adlı kendi ajanının kullanıcı testlerini genişletirken, OpenAI da Dots’ın yeteneklerini artırdı. Alphabet’in Google birimi ise bu hafta Tasks adını verdiği ajanını yeniledi. Apple’ın platformunun işletim sistemlerinin arayüzlerinde otonom olarak hareket edebilmesi de planlanıyor.
Şirket özellikle ChatGPT ve Muse gibi araçların Mac bilgisayarları kontrol etmesini sağlayan teknolojiye benzer “genel amaçlı bilgisayar kullanım ajanları” geliştirdiğini belirtti. Gizlilik de projenin temel unsurlarından biri. Apple, kullanıcı adına kod çalıştırabilen, kimlik bilgilerini kullanabilen ve işlem yapabilen ajanların güçlü izin sistemleri, güvenlik önlemleri ve şeffaflık gerektirdiğini söyledi.

Earlier this week at the DealBook conference in New York, Elon Musk, beamed in from a trip to China with President Donald Trump, was asked about the ouster of his longtime friend, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Musk compared it to kicking Michael Jordan off the Chicago Bulls’ roster during his historic run. Of Nvidia’s employees, he said, “They love [Huang]. They love him.”
Well, maybe not all of them. Thousands of employees have signed a letter asking for Huang’s return, but others tell The New York Times he ruled through praise and fear, and also by humiliating people.
According to the Times, Huang told subordinates that Nvidia’s wealth meant it wasn’t possible to motivate them with money, so humiliation was the only lever left. He reportedly told one executive his mother should have aborted him, and told another employee he would rip his arms off and beat him to death with them.
Naturally, over a 33-year career, regrettable things may have been said, but the Times found a long paper trail that suggests the incidents weren’t isolated. In 2005, for example, Michael Winston, a former HR chief, threatened to sue and called Huang’s conduct the most abusive he’d seen. Nvidia paid him more than $1 million. Huang’s spokesman calls the allegations fabrications.

State attorney says scandal ‘raises bright red flags’ and aims to find out if company misled investors
California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.
Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” said Bonta.
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: companies cannot mislead their investors.”
The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.
Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China .
Megaspeed has said it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the company late last year.
Bonta said the investigation would also look at whether the former Nvidia chief’s actions resulted in confidential information being passed to China.
“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information,” he said. “And if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law.”
Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Huang admitted the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low at the close of trading on Thursday, and wiping almost $1tn off its market value.
Earlier this week, Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair, said the company had no intention of reinstating Huang after the former CEO said he would be “honoured” to return. Elon Musk and a host of tech bosses had campaigned for Nvidia to bring him back .
Huang is due to testify before several congressional committees over the potential breach of national security on 1 December.
Shares in rival chipmaker AMD closed down almost 8% on Thursday after the publication of reports connected to short seller Hunterbrook warning about its links to China and the “circular financing” of customers.
The company, which has been targeted amid the Nvidia scandal, is looking at a further fall of more than 5% in pre-market trading.
Hunterbrook Media published allegations on the use of AMD’s software by a Chinese server maker blacklisted by the US. Sister publication, The Bear Cave newsletter, alleged that AMD’s use of datacentre lease guarantees and backstops for unsold cloud computing capacity could leave it exposed to a pullback in AI spending.
AMD said the reports’ claims “misrepresent AMD’s business practices and relationships”.
“AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations,” the company said. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity.”
AMD’s share price has more than doubled so far this year, giving the company a market capitalisation of more than $800m.

The EP/BC–1 can wirelessly stream audio to Bluetooth headphones or multiple devices using Auracast.
Teenage Engineering announced what it describes as “a modern take on a classic CD player” with its new EP/BC–1 featuring a slab-like design that leaves the spinning disc exposed instead of hiding it under a lid or inside a slide-out tray. The company says the EP/BC–1 is the first entry in its new broadcast series of products and was designed to bring “physical audio formats into a modern context, evolved from a shared obligation within the company to preserve the formats they grew up with.”
The EP/BC-1 is available now through Teenage Engineering’s online store for $299. The CD player joins the company’s existing EP–series of audio devices and has the same dimensions as its KO II synthesizer that launched in 2023 so it can be paired with, and connected to, other Teenage Engineering gear including the recently-announced EP-35 battery-powered amp .
Although it’s designed to play a nearly 45 year old medium, the EP/BC-1 features modern conveniences like variable speed playback, cue markers, a jog wheel for forward and reverse search, and built-in beat detection. There’s a very retro-looking series of digital displays showing track, index, time information, and audio levels, and around the edges you’ll find both digital and analog audio connections including a headphone jack and a USB 2.0 port.
If you want to go completely wireless the CD player has a rechargeable battery and supports both Bluetooth connections to headphones and Auracast streaming to multiple devices that support it. The EP/BC-1 is compatible with standard CDs as well as discs full of MP3 files, and when using the former it can rip tracks to 44.1 Hz/16-bit WAV files. If you want MP3s or other formats, you’ll need to convert them yourself.

An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field.
Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website , Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday .
The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.
A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof:
I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof 1 of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.
The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August , but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.”
Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules , a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.”
In the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture , a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids.
OpenAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Alpöge had been working on the problem with New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude.
OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt. The result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal recognition. But the achievement has been marred by allegations of questionable research practices, including claims it used unpublished work from mathematicians who had shared their research with its AI tools. OpenAI has strongly denied wrongdoing, but this has done little to quell the uproar.
Though most of the spotlight has been on OpenAI’s movement in math, Alpöge said in July that he solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude. The deluge of findings has left mathematicians scrambling to digest the material and figure out where they belong in what is rapidly becoming a profoundly different mathematical landscape.
