Robot vacuums are more expensive than ever, with many models from popular brands like Dyson and Shark starting at $1,200. But you usually don't have to pay such a high price tag for a great model—you just have to wait for a good sale, and with early Black Friday deals already kicking off, it's one of the best times to shop for one.
One of our favorite robot vacuum brands, Roborock , began its early Black Friday deals yesterday, and some of our favorite models we've tested are available for the best prices we've seen. Here's which models I'd snatch up while the prices are low.
The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro launched in late summer as the newest addition to the brand's more affordable Qrevo line, and it quickly landed as a pick on my guide to the Best Robot Vacuums . It's often on sale for around $600, and thanks to Black Friday it's down to the lowest price I've seen it for: $450, nearly half off.
Overall, Roborock's vacuums are great, but I've been especially impressed by this one's corner cleaning, thanks to its extendable mop arm. It won't always spot cords, but it does a better job at navigating furniture and getting underneath my cabinets than more expensive robot vacuums I've tested.
If you'd rather have a roller-mop-style robot vacuum, the Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow is another great option from Roborock's Qrevo line. This one came out in January of this year, and our reviewer instantly loved it .
The Qrevo Curv 2 Flow is a more expensive robot vacuum than the Qrevo 2 since it comes with the brand's SpriaFlow roller-mop. The internal roller spans nearly the entire width of the vacuum and can extend to edge-clean your home. It even has a built-in scraper to move dirty water into the tank instead of rolling it back onto the floor. If you're looking for an affordable mopping powerhouse, this is the one to choose. It's also nearly half off, down to $600 off the $1,000 price tag.
There's the affordable Qrevo line from Roborock, and then there's the higher-end Saros line. While both I and former WIRED reviewer Adrienne So weren't particularly impressed with the Saros 20, I've been much happier with the performance of the Saros 20 Flow. Like the Curv 2 Flow, it has a roller mop instead of spinning mop pads and did well in my mopping tests. It also didn't leave debris around, even with its high suction of 36,000 Pa.
It's one of Roborock's most expensive vacuums, and it comes across while using it—it feels very premium. I've been preferring it over the new Dyson robot vacuum I've been testing. Luckily, you can get it on sale right now for Black Friday. It still isn't cheap at $1,300, but it's one of my all-time favorites and one I have kept coming back to after trying other models.
If you're looking for something truly unique in a robot vacuum, Roborock's Saros Z70 might be what you're looking for. It has a mechanical arm built into it to pick up small items like socks while it vacuums, which feels handy, but didn't work as well as we'd hoped during testing. Still, maybe you feel that's the solution you've been dying for. If that's the case, it's available for a nice discount right now at $950.
It also packs 22,000 Pa of suction (not as powerful as the Saros 20 Flow, but still plenty of suction to clean carpets and rugs alike!) and still executes fast, effective cleaning. But the battery life on this vacuum isn't as long as that of other Roborocks we've tested. Again, you're mostly getting this one for the mechanical arm.

İspanya hükümeti, veri merkezleri için yeni bir düzenleme kabul etti. Bu düzenleme, bu altyapıların büyümesini elektrik sisteminin kapasitesi ve ülkenin çevre taahhütleriyle uyumlu hale getirmek amacıyla, yenilenebilir enerji tüketimi için şartlar , su ve enerji verimliliği ve dijital egemenlik hükümleri belirliyor.
Bakanlar Kurulu tarafından bu cuma kabul edilen Kraliyet Kararnamesi , veri merkezlerinin elektrik tüketimlerinin yüzde 80'inin yenilenebilir kaynaklardan geldiğini belgelendirmesini , üretim ile tüketim arasında saatlik eşleştirme sağlamasını ve yeni temiz üretim kapasitesini teşvik etmek için ilave üretim kapasitesi kriterlerine uymasını şart koşuyor.
Düzenleme, uzun vadeli tedarik sözleşmelerini, öz tüketimi ve enerji depolamayı kapsıyor. Ayrıca, elektrik şebekesinin istikrarını garanti etmek gerektiğinde bağlantının öncelikli olarak kesilmesi olasılığını kabul eden işletmeciler için isteğe bağlı bir geçici rejim de getiriyor.
Düzenleme, veri merkezlerinin su ve elektrik tüketimine geçici sınırlar getiriyor. Veri merkezleri suyu daha verimli kullanmak ve Avrupa kriterleri netleşene kadar çalışmalarını sürdürmek için gereken enerjiyi azaltmak zorunda olacak. Ayrıca, Avrupa mevzuatının öngördüğü bilgi şeffaflığı ile su ve enerji verimliliğine ilişkin diğer yükümlülükleri ulusal hukuk düzenine aktarıyor ve bunları İspanya'nın özgün koşullarına uyarlıyor.
Düzenleme, daha büyük ölçekli tesisler için sürdürülebilirlik konusunda bilgi verme yükümlülükleri getiriyor ve Ulusal Güvenlik Şeması'nın yüksek kategorili bilgi sistemleri için özel veri koruma ve dijital egemenlik şartları belirliyor.
Bu hallerde, en hassas verilerin Avrupa Ekonomik Alanı içinde kalması gerekecek ve üçüncü ülkelerden yönetim, bakım ve destek faaliyetlerine erişim üzerindeki kontroller güçlendirilecek.
Belirli yükümlülüklere uyulmaması, ekonomik tazminatlara ve yaptırımlara yol açabilecek; bunlar arasında elektrik şebekesine erişim ve bağlantı haklarının en fazla üç yıl süreyle askıya alınması da yer alıyor. Halihazırda değerlendirme sürecinde bulunan projeler, genel olarak, yeni koşullara uyum sağlamak için altı aylık bir süreye sahip olacak.
Karar, İspanya'da dijital altyapı talebinin güçlü bir şekilde arttığı bir dönemde alındı. İspanya hükümetinin üçüncü başbakan yardımcısı ve Ekolojik Geçiş Bakanı Sara Aagesen, veri merkezlerinin 15 gigavat (GW) elektrik erişim kapasitesine sahip olduğunu, başka 20 GW'nin ise bekleme listesinde bulunduğunu belirtti.
Aagesen, kontrol önlemleri olmadan bu tesislerin genişlemesinin elektrik sisteminde yıllık 5 milyar euroya kadar ek maliyet yaratabileceği uyarısında bulundu. Hükümetin tahminlerine göre bunun 4 milyar euroluk kısmı toptan elektrik fiyatlarına etkiden, 1 milyar euroluk kısmı ise kapasite mekanizmalarından kaynaklanacak.
Enerji Geçişi Bakanı Sara Aagesen, "Bu Kraliyet Kararnamesi olmadan faturalarımızda 5 milyar euro tutarında bir etki olurdu," diye vurguladı. Aagesen, "Farklı senaryolarımız var, ancak bu, örneğin sanayi tüketicilerinin tükettikleri elektrik için yüzde 25 daha fazla ödemesine yol açardı," diye ekledi. Bu rakamlar, hükümetin varsayımsal bir senaryoya ilişkin öngörüleri dir; henüz gerçekleşmiş maliyetleri ya da yeni düzenlemeyle garanti altına alınmış tasarrufları ifade etmiyor.
Buna paralel olarak hükümet, 2030'a kadar elektrik şebekesi için yeni bir planlama da onayladı. Plan, altyapıyı genişletmek ve güçlendirmek ile talep artışını karşılamak için 17.142 milyon euro tutarında yatırım öngörüyor. Plan, veri merkezlerindeki tüketimler de dahil olmak üzere yeni tüketimler için kapasite ayırsa da, özel olarak bu tesislere odaklanmıyor.
İspanya, yenilenebilir enerji kaynakları, bağlantı imkanları ve Avrupa'daki stratejik konumundan yararlanarak kendisini veri merkezleri alanında uluslararası yatırımlar için bir cazibe merkezi olarak pekiştirmek istiyor.
Yeni düzenleme, bu büyümeyi daha yüksek enerji ve çevresel verimliliğe bağlı hale getirmeyi amaçlıyor. Elektrik, su ve bağlantı kapasitesinin erişilebilirliği, bu tesislerin geliştirilmesi için başlıca belirleyici faktörlerden biri haline gelmiş durumda. Devam eden projeler ve gelecekteki yatırımlar üzerindeki etki, yeni yükümlülüklerin nasıl uygulanacağına ve nihai metinde öngörülen süreler ile koşullara bağlı olacak.

If you’re wondering how Alex Ridha’s (aka Boys Noize) collaboration with Nine Inch Nails influenced his new record 7LLVSION , the answer is simple: It didn’t. That’s not to say Ridha didn’t learn anything from the virtuosic production team of Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, but most of the songs on 7LLVSION had been knocking around for some time. And as Ridha is quick to point out, these are not rock songs built for live performance; they’re “battle tested” for clubs and DJ sets. “I was kind of back on the usual kind of thing,” he tells The Verge .
“I do the same I kind of always do. I go make coffee, go in my room, put on the machines, and I’ll start messing around with sounds and build one sound to another and there comes a record,” he says. Like previous Boys Noize releases, a lot of 7LLVSION starts with sound design. “It’s kind of tech-driven, in a way,” he says, “because I always look for the newest machines.”
On 7LLVSION, Ridha frequently turned to an obscure Italian semimodular synth, the Grp A4 . “It’s just so powerful , and it sounds so big,” he says. The routing options, dual filters (which he uses in parallel), and built-in sequencer kept leading him to new and inspiring places. Because of that, the A4 ended up on a number of tracks, including “ Shut It Down ,” “ 1+1+1 ,” and “Ycore.”.
“The exciting part is always to, you know, not repeat myself, even with the drum sounds, and try something new that I haven’t tried before,” Ridha says. For a few tracks, that meant getting away from the rigid, quantized grooves of techno and opting for a more dynamic, live feeling on tracks like “Shut It Down” and “1+1+1” especially. “Live drums are the new 808,” he says.
He looked to German bands of the ’70s and ’80s for inspiration, like Can , Amon Düül , and Deutsch Amerikanische Freundschaft . He also called out Conny Plank, who produced landmark records by Neu!, Kraftwerk, and Eurythmics. But in general he says, “My goal is to not sound like anything you can point to. You know, I don’t want to be a direct copy.” Instead, he was chasing the sound of “electronic punk.” That means aggressive basslines, driving drums, and stripped-down arrangements that avoid overstuffing the mix with too many instruments.
But it all comes back to the club at the end of the day. “Environment has always been the main thing in my music. I need to have a record that I want to play at the party,” he says, and that meant testing the songs off 7LLVSION extensively in his DJ sets and letting the audience tell him what works and what doesn’t. “The club is the most open and objective situation you can have,” he says. “They don’t know what I’m playing, so they hear something for the first time, and you can just look at someone’s face, or someone’s there in the room to get a cool reaction, and that usually makes me feel good about something or not.”
Boys Noize is currently touring the world on the festival circuit, and 7LLVSION is available now on most major streaming services .

Avrupa'da çocuk hakları alanında faaliyet gösteren sivil toplum kuruluşlarını bir araya getiren Eurochild, "Avrupa'da İhtiyaç Sahibi Çocuklara İlişkin 2026 Raporu"nu yayımladı.
Türkiye'nin de aralarında bulunduğu 32 ülkeden 54 üye ve katkı sağlayıcının değerlendirmeleriyle hazırlanan raporda, çocuk yoksulluğu, sosyal koruma sistemleri, temel hizmetlere erişim ve çocuklara ayrılan kamu kaynakları ele alındı.
Raporda, Avrupa İstatistik Ofisinin (Eurostat) 2025 verilerine göre, Avrupa Birliği (AB) ülkelerinde çocukların yüzde 24,3'ünün yoksulluk veya sosyal dışlanma riski altında olduğu, bu oranın 2024'teki sınırlı düşüşün ardından yeniden yükseldiği belirtildi.
AB ülkeleri arasında en yüksek oran yüzde 33,8 ile İspanya'da kaydedilirken, bu ülkeyi yüzde 33,1 ile Bulgaristan ve yüzde 32,4 ile Romanya izledi.
Çocuk yoksulluğunun 2024'e kıyasla 10 ülkede arttığı, 15 ülkede azaldığı ve 2 ülkede değişmediği aktarılan raporda, en yüksek artışların Avusturya, Estonya ve İrlanda'da görüldüğü kaydedildi.
En belirgin düşüşlerin ise Hırvatistan, Malta ve Hollanda'da yaşandığı bildirildi.
Raporda, AB'ye aday ve potansiyel aday ülkelerde çocuk yoksulluğu riskinin genel olarak daha yüksek seyrettiği, Arnavutluk'ta 2023 verilerine göre çocukların yüzde 46,6'sının yoksulluk veya sosyal dışlanma riski altında bulunduğu ifade edildi.
Ukrayna'da ise çocukların yüzde 70'inin temel mal ve hizmetlere erişemediği belirtildi.
Raporda, tek ebeveynli ve kalabalık ailelerde yaşayan çocuklar ile göçmen, mülteci, Roman ve engelli çocukların yoksulluk ve sosyal dışlanma riskinden daha fazla etkilendiği vurgulandı.
Avrupa genelinde çocuklara yönelik sosyal koruma sistemlerinin finansmanında önemli eksiklikler bulunduğuna işaret edilen raporda, sosyal yardımların artan yaşam maliyetlerine ayak uyduramadığı ve karmaşık idari süreçlerin ailelerin desteklere erişimini zorlaştırdığı kaydedildi.
Raporda özellikle erken çocukluk eğitimi, bakım hizmetleri, ruh sağlığı desteği ve uygun fiyatlı konut alanlarında yatırımların yetersiz kaldığı belirtildi.
Ayrıca raporda çocuklara yönelik hizmetlerin kısa vadeli projelere ve geçici finansman kaynaklarına bağımlı olmasının sosyal koruma sistemlerinin sürdürülebilirliğini olumsuz etkilediği ifade edildi.
Eurochild raporda AB'nin 2028-2034 dönemini kapsayan uzun vadeli bütçesinde çocuk yoksulluğuyla mücadele için en az 20 milyar avro kaynak ayrılması çağrısında bulundu.
Raporda, AB'nin gelecek dönem ulusal ve bölgesel ortaklık planlarının en az yüzde 25'inin sosyal kapsayıcılığa ayrılması, çocuk yoksulluğuyla mücadele için de en az yüzde 5 oranında özel kaynak tahsis edilmesi önerildi.
Çocuk yoksulluğunun yüksek olduğu ülkelerde bu oranın yüzde 10'a çıkarılması istendi.

Early in Shakespeare’s tragedy Julius Caesar , the title character is publicly offered a crown as a symbol of absolute power. Caesar refuses it three times, dramatically fainting after the final try. Scholars say that Caesar’s “falling sickness,” as his eventual assassin Brutus put it, masked his true intention to rule. His effort to win over the crowd with his humility only intensified the momentum to grant him more power. Indeed, after his refusal, his adherents became even more impassioned, setting the stage for his eventual claim to kingship. “If Caesar had stabb’d their mothers, they would have done no less,” said a Roman senator of the sycophantic crowd.
Jensen Huang was not so strategic. He did not even wait until a crown was offered before grabbing for it. On November 12, Nvidia’s cofounder had resigned from his post as CEO, promising to work to heal his family and earn back trust. The reasons were obvious. He had been engaging in an affair with an alleged Chinese spy . Under his leadership, billions of dollars ’ worth of Nvidia’s sales had gone to her formerly obscure company in Singapore, which, in a potential violation of export regulations, the company used to power Chinese AI efforts. In addition, he was carrying on an affair with an Nvidia subordinate (or was it two ?), itself a fireable transgression. Nonetheless, because of his success in building Nvidia, Huang has been receiving a noisy groundswell of support from Silicon Valley and Wall Street, with the same loyalty as the crowd that would have idolized Caesar even if he’d stabbed their mothers.
Huang, used to exercising power, seemed as energized as the mob supporting Caesar had been. Social media was exploding with memes portraying him as a hero whose return would result in Homeric redemption. Silicon Valley leaders like Travis Kalanick, Tim Sweeney, and Elon Musk called his removal an injustice that must be addressed. One of Huang’s talents is moving fast. So perhaps he used state-of-the-art Rubin GPUs to dispatch an armada of AI introspection-bots, fast-tracking what formerly would have taken months of moral cleansing into a few days. In any case, on November 17, when the pixels on his resignation message had barely settled, he returned to X to announce that he would be honored to reclaim his position if offered.
It was not to be. Within hours, Nvidia’s board threw more water on Huang’s overture than a Texas data center consumes in a year. During a scheduled earnings call, chair Harvey Jones said, “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation but does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.” Nvidia’s interim leader, Colette Kress, who had been its long-time CFO, ended the call with a devastating kicker: “We’ve got this.” Et tu, Colette?
The search for a replacement will proceed. But even after the board presumably closed the door, and Kress told employees in an all-hands meeting once again that “we got this,” the push to restore him has not quieted. The president of the United States hasn’t retracted his opinion that Huang should resume his post. A petition called “Stand With Jensen” now has over 200,000 signatures. Hedge funder Bill Ackman zinged out a hysterical X post this week charging “major governance failures by directors.” (Clearly, Ackman’s view of ideal governance is no governance.) Most alarmingly, Semafor has reported that Huang himself had spoken to at least one board member about his reinstatement and that several directors may still be open to the possibility. At press time, Huang has not given any public indication that he is no longer angling for a triumphant return.
At the New York Times DealBook conference, held a day after the earnings call, the Jensen affair dominated the discussion, even as Anthropic was readying the biggest IPO in history. On stage, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Greg Brockman expressed admiration for Huang but did not recommend his reinstatement. But Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey said that “nobody can take Jensen’s place in this critical juncture” because “his personal relations are the reason everyone is willing to do business” with Nvidia. Elon Musk reaffirmed his outrage that Huang had been forced out, saying it was like the Chicago Bulls firing Michael Jordan in his prime during a playoff hot streak. In my informal conversations during breaks, I found people on both sides of the divide. One person was a substantial Nvidia investor who showed me pictures of themselves with Huang. Like many with a financial stake in the company, this individual was eager to see Huang back in charge.
Everyone is in agreement that the Huang story is tragic. But the outcry for Huang’s reinstatement is a broader tragedy, revealing how greed has eclipsed ethics and patriotism. Those clamoring for reinstatement have one argument: that Huang’s leadership was so singular and superlative that he must keep his job. Not doing so would dishonor his previous efforts and degrade Nvidia’s future performance. Essentially, it’s an ends-justifies-the-means rationale incompatible with corporate oversight and even fidelity to law and national security.
The push to reinstate Huang is also a grotesque extension of the cult of the founder, which assumes that those who built a company have unique abilities to run it and should be unconstrained in how they do so. (Serious question: If founders are so great, why do the vast majority of startups fail ?)
There’s no question that Huang has built one of the greatest companies ever and delivered historic returns to shareholders. But one irony of the Bring Back Jensen Movement is that this crisis has exposed him, in some respects, as an erratic, even a lousy, CEO. His personal indiscretions cost shareholders almost a trillion dollars! He lied to his board. He pursued a strategy that seems to have violated the spirit if not the law of export regulations. He gave senior executive posts to family members who pursued a passion in the chip business later in life, including his daughter (trained as a chef), son (went to art school and owned a cocktail lounge), and son-in-law (former professional skier). In a public company, nepotism comes at shareholders’ expense.
On top of that, he failed in a critical duty of a CEO—preparing a succession plan. Nvidia has none, solely because Huang acted as if he would run it forever. At DealBook, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, after the obligatory expressions of empathy toward Huang, threw some shade on leaders who don’t plan for their departure: “People get old and die,” he said. “If a company will succeed, it needs someone to take over. I’ve never trusted a leader, founder or otherwise, who says the institution after I left was completely gone. Like, then what did you build?”
Finally, if Huang were so passionate about Nvidia’s future, why is he still angling for a return? The possibility, even a remote one, that he will be reinstated may discourage the best candidates from considering an offer to lead Nvidia. Huang would best serve Nvidia by shutting down the talk from his Silicon Valley cronies and demanding that the Bring Jensen Back petition be scrapped.
Ultimately, by giving up his quest to reclaim the crown, Huang would better serve not only Nvidia but himself. His energy should be devoted first to mending his family relations and then working with lawyers to maintain his reputation, fortune, and maybe even freedom. There’s an additional bonus to his departure. He will be leaving Nvidia at a peak for high-powered GPU chips and AI’s economic power. If the bubble does pop, Huang will avoid being the face of AI when the fall comes. Remember, things didn’t work out too well for Julius Caesar.

Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet company. This time, it’s the email marketing firm Mailchimp, bought for $3.68 billion from the tax-preparation giant Intuit.
Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell.
Flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the company’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the new cash will be used to repurchase shares.
Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock.
Still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game plan to hold them long term. In just the last year, the company has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable, and Miro . Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup, and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources.
“We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July .

The director of Minotaur says there is no politics in Russia.
The year is 2022. Vladimir Putin has announced the military draft. In Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur , set in the fictional town of Krasoborsk, a quietly unhappy couple, called Gleb and Galina, carry on with their lives, or try to, geopolitics notwithstanding. For Galina, carrying on means an affair, which we deduce from a scene of her texting with a faint smile, her face lit in the dark by the light of her phone. ( Minotaur is a remake of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 film The Unfaithful Wife, whose title gives the plot away more readily than Zvyagintsev’s.)
Meanwhile, Gleb runs a kind of private contracting concern and is soon asked to scare up military recruits to meet a quota. At this point, the domestic noir and the workplace drama merge to dramatic, devastating, and darkly funny effects.
In Minotaur , as in his five other features, Zvyagintsev has the camera moving seemingly objectively, almost omnisciently, putting the characters in their context. Occasionally they appear rather small, especially when set against the epic scale of their mythic and biblical fates. That the environment shapes the person seems to be a recurring revelation across all six of his staggering films. Minotaur, too, opens with a natural landscape of the arboreal kind and ends with another, different landscape, of clouds. In the middle is a movie about people trying to make sense of the landscapes they find themselves in, of the social, moral, relational variety.
Zvyagintsev has some experience with finding oneself in incomprehensible landscapes. After receiving Russia’s Sputnik V covid-19 vaccine during the pandemic, he fell ill, and later learned about the invasion of Ukraine while recovering from a medical coma in Germany. He subsequently chose not to return home, moving to France.
At the Cannes Film Festival in May, Minotaur won the second-highest honor. In his acceptance speech, Zvyagintsev spoke about the war, saying: “The only person who can stop this butchery is the President of the Russian Federation. Put an end to this carnage. The whole world is waiting for it.” While he resists the identity of exile, in September the Russian government designated him a “foreign agent.”
Zvyagintsev returned this year to the New York Film Festival, where he last visited with his 2014 film Leviathan , which won a Golden Globe and was nominated for an Oscar. His debut in 2003, The Return , won a top prize at Venice International Film Festival, after which he was invited to meet Putin, an account of which appears in his forthcoming book. Out of his six films, four have won prestigious prizes at Cannes, including Elena and Loveless .
We discussed the three years he spent cleaning the streets of Moscow in the early 1990s, his status as a Russian immigrant in France now, and how he captures that great Chekhovian instinct: that life is wretched, but what can we do, we must go on living. Zvyagintsev spoke to The Verge through a translator from Los Angeles.
I understand you went from cleaning streets to making commercials. What happened in between?
It kind of happened almost at the same time, because I was cleaning the streets to be able to live in Moscow. From 1990 to 1993, I was cleaning the streets. And then I was going to the Museum of Cinema and watching a movie every single day. Those were my formative years, when I learned a lot about cinema.
I had been living in a huge communal flat, free accommodation in a beautiful historic mansion in central Moscow. It was a really big apartment, and there were three street cleaners, including me, that lived there. In 1993, I was forced to leave the apartment after someone from the local housing administration decided to take it over. The two others had families, so they decided that if someone was supposed to move, it was going to be me, since I was single.
I was offered alternative accommodation, but realized that the only reason I had continued working as a street sweeper was to keep that particular apartment.
So the first night when I had to leave the apartment, I left it fast without an actual plan. I had to spend the night inside a truck that was abandoned and that was parked in the street.
I got a new job as a guard, as a night guard at a kindergarten where I also ate leftover food from the children’s meals.
After the first day, I called my friend who was working in commercials and doing music videos. I asked him to help with a job, because I was sure I was able to shoot commercials. After the first commercial, I met some producers who liked my work, and then I started shooting commercials on the regular and working as a freelance for some time. One of those commercials was noticed by a producer from a TV channel called REN TV, who was shooting a bunch of TV series at the time. His name was Dmitry Lesnevsky and he asked me whether I wanted to shoot movies, and I said it was my dream. And then Dmitry presented me with 15 scripts of choice, and I shot three episodes of a television series called The Black Room for this channel, each 25 minutes long.
We were army friends. He was a close friend from the army. He was a cinema mechanic. He was starting movies for the soldiers when they were in the army. They had a theater, and I was in the music ensemble in the army. He was also an actor.
You had an adverse reaction to a covid vaccine. You were ill for a long time. You nearly died. You moved, and eventually settled in France. You’ve said you can’t know how that experience changed you as a filmmaker, but I’m curious if you know how that experience changed you as a person.
I got sick in Russia. I was in a coma for 40 days in Germany. I had a major problem with my lungs, a bacteria called klebsiella found its way there. They thought that they would need a lung transplant. Fortunately, the Germans were able to operate, and the transplant was not needed. I moved to France a year later after the coma.
What was the biggest change for me was the rhythm of life. I understood that you cannot lose time, so I’m trying to do things in a much more dynamic manner, and not leave things for later because we don’t know if this later exists. So that that’s the biggest change, really, just seeing life as something that passes by quickly.
You are a vocal opponent of the current Russian government. Do you consider yourself to be in political exile?
I am not in political exile. I did not have that status, and I never applied for it because I don’t see any necessity for that. I consider myself an immigrant. I’ve been living away from my native country for almost five years, but I did not leave on purpose. I was already in Europe when the war happened. There is a term in Russian, called nevozvrashchenets, which means a person who does not come back, someone who has left their home country and has not returned, particularly for political reasons. I was in the clinic in Germany and then in France when the war started, and I realized that I could not go back to the country that is at war.
You’ve said you are not political, but your movies seem overtly political, to me. You’ve also said that the job of an artist is to reflect reality. You don’t think you’re political, but your job is to reflect reality, and we are living at a time when politics is dominant. How do you reconcile all this?
It’s very simple to reconcile. It’s just that the politics barges into our lives, and we have to reflect what’s going on in the world. You become a witness of what’s going on beyond your window, what’s going on to the environment, to the world around you, to the world close to you. It just so happens that the politics dominate our lives. We are witnessing historical events that we cannot not reflect in the movies.
“There is no politics in Russia, in the sense of politics being a struggle for power, dialogue between different parties or worldviews… This does not exist in Russia. There’s only one power”

Agreements aim to simplify trade checks, link emissions systems and launch a youth mobility programme.
The United Kingdom and the European Union have struck a deal aimed at mending fences and repairing the economic fallout caused by Brexit, a decade after UK voters opted to leave the bloc.
At a joint news conference following the EU-UK summit in Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the deal would “rebuild the bridges that were broken all those years ago”. He hailed the agreements as “a good deal for Britain”.
Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, said there was an “intensive” debate on how much the world has changed since Brexit, during the meeting.
The COVID pandemic “was not even over when Russia started the war in Ukraine”, she said. “We have stuck together from day one on.
“We can always work on an incremental improvement of our relationship, but as I said, we are totally open to do the necessary brainstorming for the wider picture.”
The agreements cover three areas – easing trade restrictions, expanding opportunities for young people to live and work across borders, and addressing carbon levies.
But disagreements remain, particularly over university tuition fees.
Burnham also faces political resistance at home over how far strengthening ties with the EU should go.
Three main agreements were on the table at the summit between Burnham and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa.
The first would remove checks and reduce paperwork on food and agricultural products traded between Britain and the EU, making exports easier and potentially lowering costs for businesses and consumers. That could be good news for businesspeople like Tim Jones , an English cheesemaker whom Al Jazeera recently interviewed.
The second would link the two sides’ emissions-trading systems, which would give an exemption to goods from Britain and the EU, such as steel, from each other’s border carbon levies.
The third establishes a youth mobility programme allowing up to 100,000 people under 30 from each side to live in the other’s territory for up to three years for work, study or travel.
Burnham said the agreements could add 0.5 percent to Britain’s gross domestic product (GDP), raising his previous estimate of 0.4 percent.
The prime minister described the package as a way of “cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people”.
Despite the breakthrough, hurdles remain, among them university tuition fees. Brussels wants EU students attending British universities to pay the same domestic rates as British students rather than the substantially higher international fees currently charged.
London has resisted the proposal, which could have significant financial implications for universities.
“We have not yet reached an agreement on tuition fees, and we have given ourselves six months to reach that agreement,” an EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters.
Another unresolved issue concerns Britain’s demand for access to the EU’s “made in Europe” rules, notably for cars.
“Made in Europe” is part of the EU’s planned Industrial Accelerator Act and is aimed primarily at forcing Chinese automakers to produce cars within the bloc using local suppliers in order to qualify for key subsidies and bid for government procurement contracts.
The EU has indicated it is willing to grant this but on the condition that London aligns with its policies, which restrict imports of Chinese electric vehicles.
Burnham has indicated that his government will examine longer-term options, ranging from maintaining existing arrangements to joining the EU customs union or eventually rejoining the bloc.
“After the summit, we will initiate a discussion with our EU partners about options for our long-term relationship,” he said.
But rejoining would require support from British voters and unanimous approval from EU member states, making any immediate return unlikely.
Al Jazeera’s Rosie Birchard, reporting from Brussels, said there was “no actual signing” expected on Friday. “There’s no document being inked,” she said.
A UK government spokesperson told Al Jazeera, “As with all international agreements, there is a legal process in each respective country which will now take place … and talks will continue on some areas.”
Within Burnham’s Labour Party, some politicians support rebuilding European ties but fear reopening the divisive Brexit debate.
“I’m happy with closer ties, but he does need to tread carefully,” one Labour MP told the AFP news agency.
The opposition Conservatives and Nigel Farage’s Reform UK have predictably criticised the government’s direction. “I’m afraid that the great Brexit debate has just started again,” Farage, who led the Brexit campaign, told the BBC.
He warned that the discussion would soon become one about whether Britain should rejoin the EU.
A YouGov poll published on Wednesday suggested 54 percent of UK citizens think “it would be acceptable to have a rejoin referendum in the next five years” but are divided over whether it is a top priority.
European officials, meanwhile, have remained cautious about Britain’s longer-term intentions.
Sonja Hyland, Ireland’s ambassador in London, said there was “a lack of clarity” about what Brexit meant. If Britain wants to reopen negotiations, she said, it must “make a clear decision as to what it wants”.

The ICJ has held Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya and ordered restitution and reparations. Community members have hailed the ruling, but caution that achieving real change will be long and hard.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the country's Rohingya community a decade ago, in a historic judgment hailed by the long-persecuted minority and rights groups.
The United Nations' top court also ordered the Myanmar government to prevent a repeat of the crimes , undertake legal reforms to protect the Rohingya and provide the victims with reparations or, where it cannot, compensate them.
The judgment came seven years after The Gambia filed the case with the court , accusing Buddhist-majority Myanmar of a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder against the country's predominantly Muslim Rohingya community in 2016 and 2017.
It is the ICJ's first finding of genocide against a state, and the first ruling in any of the cases filed against Myanmar or its leaders in multiple courts around the world.
Lucky Karim was 14 when she and her mother and brothers were forced to flee their village in Rakhine State to escape the Myanmar military's advance in August 2017.
She joined the roughly 700,000 other Rohingya who crossed the border into Bangladesh at the time.
Now a prominent Rohingya activist, Karim heard the court's judgment in person in The Hague.
"For me … it's a very personal day, a personal moment, as someone who survived and escaped genocide in 2017. It took nearly a decade for the world to finally hear our voice," she said.
"For generations the [Myanmar] military stripped away our identity, our citizenship, tried to erase us from our homeland, told the world that what they did to us in 2017 was merely clearance operations, or worse, that we didn't even exist," said Wai Wai Nu, another Rohingya activist and former political prisoner.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Today, she said, their decades of persecution "is actually validated, and the truth has come out."
Tun Khin, a Rohingya activist and plaintiff in a universal jurisdiction case against Myanmar in Argentina , called the judgment "a historic moment" and "a big day for the Rohingya."
The press bureau of the Myanmar president's office did not respond to DW's requests for comment. The government's main mouthpiece, the state-run New Light of Myanmar newspaper, made no mention of the ruling online.
Throughout the trial, Myanmar claimed that its actions in Rakhine State were strictly part of legitimate counterinsurgency operations against the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, an armed group in the area that had been attacking police and military posts.
The ICJ flatly rejected the argument. "The court views casualties and damage far in excess of what was justified by military necessity," ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said, reading from the 15-judge panel's 9-6 ruling in The Hague.
"The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations," he added.
A UN-backed fact-finding mission concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the pogroms. By some estimates, about 1 in 5 of them were children.
Michael Becker, an associate professor of international human rights law at Trinity College Dublin in Ireland, said the court's ruling was both historic and "monumental" not only because it found a state responsible for genocide, but also because "it demonstrates that establishing genocidal intent is not impossible."
He noted that the panel took pains to show that The Gambia's case passed the court's established "only reasonable inference" test for genocidal intent. The ruling also "helpfully affirms" that forced transfer, targeting children and sexual violence could be relevant factors, he added.
Amid elation among the Rohingya and rights groups, the focus quickly turned to making the court's prescribed remedies real.
The ICJ said Myanmar was now obliged to allow the "safe, voluntary and dignified" return of those who fled, investigate the crimes, and prosecute those found responsible. It also told Myanmar to return or replace all stolen property or, within two years, show the court it was compensating victims for what it could not.
But those behind the genocide, including former military chief and current president, Min Aung Hlaing, have remained in power since toppling Myanmar's democratically elected government in 2021.
Much of the country, including Rakhine State, is still in the midst of a brutal civil war between the military and an array of armed resistance groups . And the group that now controls most of Rakhine, the Arakan Army, is widely accused of persecuting the Rohingya as well.
"These are not conditions amenable to realizing the relief ordered by the ICJ anytime soon," said Becker.
Enforcing the court's orders ultimately falls to the UN Security Council. But China and Russia, which both back the Myanmar government and keep it well armed, would "almost certainly" veto any proposed Council resolution that aims to punish Myanmar, said Richard Horsey, senior Asia adviser at the International Crisis Group.
"Whatever pressure there is will come from governments and the General Assembly, not the Council," he said.
Immediately after Thursday's ICJ judgment, the UK said it was expelling Myanmar's defense attache in London and would call for a UN Security Council session to discuss the court's decision.
A number of Western governments have already buried Myanmar under round after round of sanctions over the past decade, but with little to no apparent effect.
Myanmar is even taking tentative steps to shake off its global pariah status and restore regular relations with the rest of the world. Min Aung Hlaing has been warmly hosted by eight Asian and Eastern European countries since arranging his transition from army general to president earlier this year following rigged elections.
Horsey said the ICJ judgment would slow those efforts but not reverse them.
"Most governments in the region will keep engaging, but those with Muslim-majority publics, especially Malaysia and Indonesia, will find it harder to justify at home," he said.
Japan and South Korea, which maintain extensive business ties with Myanmar, are likely to remain cautious, he added, while the United States, which has reportedly had recent meetings with senior government officials, would keep up a transactional relationship.
"For [Myanmar], the real cost is that every government that deals with it will now have to explain why it is engaging a state found responsible for genocide," Horsey said.
The Rohingya, meanwhile, expect a long and difficult fight for real change.
"A judgment in The Hague will not on its own stop the bombs or feed starving families or stop the atrocities in Rakhine State," said Wai Wai Nu. "It is imperative that the international community take action to enforce the ruling," she added.
Karim said other countries should use the ICJ judgment "as a tool to open every possible door to help us and protect the people on the ground."
The Gambia's lead counsel in the case, Arsalan Suleman, said the genocide ruling could be used to help hold the perpetrators to account in other courts. The International Criminal Court, for one, is weighing an arrest warrant request for Min Aung Hlaing for alleged crimes against humanity, also against the Rohingya.
Tun Khin said the wish of most Rohingya is simple, if still hard to foresee. "They want to return home, to their houses and own villages," he said, but this time with full citizenship rights and legal protection.
"It will take time," he acknowledged. "This is just the beginning."

Warehouses, railway stations, energy plants and residential buildings were hit during a night of heavy Russian strikes
Russia targeted bridges in Kyiv and railway stations overnight in a major attack launched days after Ukraine badly damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge.
Ballistic missiles hit key crossings in the capital during a nationwide assault which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said was "one of the most massive strikes" of the war so far and left at least nine dead.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for the attack on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied Crimean peninsula.
The latest Russian strikes coincided with talks around the war, and came as the Kremlin pushed back against a US claim that Russia could be open to Western-backed security guarantees for Ukraine.
The overnight attack against Ukraine was spread across several cities and regions, Zelensky said, with residential buildings and energy facilities also hit.
Air raid sirens lasted non-stop throughout the night and were ongoing into the morning.
Zelensky said over 110 missiles and more than 400 attack drones were launched by Russia, adding that "particularly insidious" tactics to launch the waves in 20 to 30-minute internals made it "more difficult to extinguish fires, clear debris, and restore services".
The three bridges targeted in Kyiv - the Podilsko-Voskresensky Bridge, the Darnytskyi Bridge and the Southern Bridge - were closed to traffic.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to "avoid travelling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary", adding to the disruption around the capital following a first round of strikes against vital crossings earlier this week.
At least seven people were killed and 17 more were injured, Klitschko added, with unspecified civilian facilities also hit.
Ukraine's major operation to take out the road section of the Crimean Bridge earlier this week was a tactical and symbolic blow for Moscow.
Since illegally annexing Crimea in 2014, Moscow has housed troops and military equipment there, with occupying forces travelling through the peninsula towards the front line.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said an operation to weaken the bridge's defences and ultimately cause part of it to collapse had been weeks in the making.
Russian President Vladimir Putin - who personally opened the bridge in 2019 to international condemnation - said the Kremlin's retaliation for the strike would be "far more painful".
Of the nine fatalities confirmed so far, seven were in Kyiv and two were in Lviv, with at least 28 people injured.
The Sknyliv railway station in Lviv, a city in western Ukraine which has become one of the primary entry points to Ukraine for people and international aid, was badly damaged, the city's Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said.
At least two people were killed in a strike on a railway station in western Ukraine
The attack began hours after European leaders including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said they were ready for negotiations involving Moscow to end the war in Ukraine.
The Berlin meeting of the so-called coalition of the willing, an international alliance of Ukraine's allies committed to providing security support in the event of a peace deal, was attended by Zelensky and US President Donald Trump's envoys.
Jared Kushner said the US "wants to make a deal with Europe by his side" after fears of an agreement negotiated between the US and Russia were reignited by Trump's one-to-one talks with Putin earlier this week.
He claimed Russia was "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on Nato's Article Five, which requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.
On Monday, Russia's deputy foreign minister Sergei Ryabkov pushed back against that, saying "quasi-Nato" membership for Ukraine would be "unacceptable" to Russia. The Kremlin has long cited the prospect of Ukraine joining Nato as a key justification for its war effort.
The US president dialled into the Berlin talks from Air Force One on his way back from China, where he met his Russian counterpart and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
He reportedly questioned the decision of European leaders to commit €70bn (£58.6bn; $76.bn) in military funding for Ukraine.
The UK and France are jointly leading the first military exercise organised by the coalition of the willing, which involves thousands of troops from 11 countries and is taking place in Poland.
On Friday, Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk accused Russia of an "intentional provocation" after a Russian cruise missile landed in his country .
It struck around 50km (31 miles) from its border with Ukraine, the Polish Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Friday.
Two more unidentified projectiles, suspected to be a drone and a second missile, landed in villages nearby and no one was harmed, he added.
Polish and Swedish jets were scrambled on Nato's eastern flank as Russia's attack on western Ukraine continued. They have since been stood down.
France's foreign minister Jean-Noël Barro has called for a meeting of the UN Security Council following Russia's attack on Kyiv.
He described the strikes, which reportedly damaged the Austrian and Dutch embassies, as "crimes" that "Russia will have to answer for".

Island Global Research said the survey was completed by more than 3,000 people across Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man
There has been "a major increase" in the overall cost of living in the past 12 months in Guernsey, Jersey and the Isle of Man, a survey has found.
Island Global Research, a market research and consultancy company, found more than 69% of respondents in Jersey, 68% in Guernsey and 70% in the Isle of Man said they had noticed a cost increase , external .
The survey, which was completed by over 1,000 people in each island, saw 57% of respondents describe themselves as "less than comfortable" with about one in 10 going without essentials like food and heating.
The survey also found 65% said they now spent less on non essentials and 53% said they are shopping around more because of the price rises.
In Jersey, 10% of respondents reported they could not afford the increased costs and often have to go with out essentials, while in Guernsey it was 11%.
The survey also showed that two thirds of people in Jersey said they had found it difficult to meet living costs in the last 12 months, an increase of 17 percentage points compared to 2024 .
Guernsey also saw an increase with 58% reporting they found it difficult to meet living costs.
The survey also found about one in four received support to help finance their everyday living expenses in the last six months.
On the Isle of Man, 36% said they cut back on groceries and 30% received support to help finance everyday living expenses over a six-month period.

Activists in more than 20 countries demonstrate over cost of living, learning conditions and rising military spending
Students and young workers have taken to the streets in more than 20 European countries in coordinated protests over the surging cost of living and housing, deteriorating learning conditions and rising military spending.
Activists from more than 50 groups in countries including Belgium, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Portugal , Spain and the UK held rallies on Friday, lighting flares, burning cardboard models of tanks and waving placards, many reading “fight for our future”.
Calling it Europe’s biggest coordinated youth protest of recent years, the Youth Strike coalition said demonstrations were planned in about 400 cities under the slogan “fight for our future, not their wars”.
It made five broad demands, including an end to militarisation and conscription; structural investment in education and welfare; solidarity with Palestine; climate and social justice, and a “radical transformation of the system we live in”.
An Italian organiser, Alessandro di Miceli, said the Europe-wide protests were “to claim our right to a better and dignified future”. Specific demands differed from country to country, he said, but were all “deeply connected between each other”.
A Portuguese organiser, Leonor Chicó, said: “As young people, we know that we must organise and fight for our future, because no one else will do it for us.” Governments “show us every day that the needs of our generation are not their priority”, she said.
Shabbir Lakha from the UK-based Stop The War coalition said the mobilisation was “a crucial step towards building a lasting international movement capable of bringing together young people, students and workers around common demands”.
After weeks of demonstrations across several countries sparked by long-running French school protests , governments are struggling to respond to growing calls for affordable housing, functioning public services and greater social equality.
Among the organisers of Friday’s rallies in France were the gilets jaunes (yellow vests), whose protests rocked the country in 2018 and 2019, while in Germany , about 1,000 students demonstrated in Berlin over fears of a return to compulsory military service.
In Rome, Milan and other Italian cities, tens of thousands protested as the country’s largest trade union, the CGIL, ⁠staged a general strike against ⁠the economic policies of the prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, which it described as the country’s call for change.
“We ​are living under a government that is cutting healthcare and education, taking away our present and trying to rob us of our future,” said Laura Peritore, 24, a university student. “We will not back down and will take our future back.”
At a youth-led demonstration in London, marchers waved banners reading: “No to war, racism, climate crisis, capitalism.” In Spain , the protests fell on the anniversary of the death of the late dictator Francisco Franco.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham returns from the UK-EU summit with a potential new deal and a new start.
A decade after the narrow vote to leave the EU, the United Kingdom is showing every sign of buyer’s remorse.
For many, the bitterly fought contest over the referendum on whether to leave the EU was unpleasant and divisive.
Couples and families reportedly split over where they stood on the referendum. Each side of the debate – Leave and Remain – became a cipher for how people saw themselves and their country in a changing world.
As the campaign unfolded amid accusations of foreign influence and dirty tricks, the murder of a politician , a debate over economics and political sovereignty, a visceral fight intensified over identity, belonging and competing visions of what it meant to be British.
Critics and pro-Brexit slammed various exit deals that successive governments negotiated with Brussels as somehow a betrayal of what had originally been a binary choice.
The EU, the trading bloc the UK sat uneasily within for nearly half a century, remains the country’s biggest trading partner.
On Friday, in a joint news conference with Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, following the latest UK-EU summit in Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham hailed the first in a series of expected deals with the EU as rebuilding “the bridges that were broken all those years ago”.
The agreements, which cover three main areas – easing trade restrictions, expanding opportunities for young people to live and work across borders, and addressing carbon levies – were characterised by Burnham as “a good deal for Britain” and regarded as first steps towards bringing the UK back into the EU’s orbit.
Some in the UK believe that leaving the single market and customs union brought little tangible benefit while creating additional paperwork, border checks and barriers to trade with the UK’s largest export market. Others have no regrets about leaving the bloc.
According to polling expert Sir John Curtice, surveys show an average of 62 percent favour rejoining, against 38 percent for staying out, once undecided respondents are excluded.
“Whatever the nuances, the UK public are certainly in a different place on the EU than [they were] in 2016,” he told Al Jazeera.
According to some analysts, the government – which is not bound by a single written constitution – could, with the EU’s agreement, begin the process of rejoining without holding another referendum, or even including the commitment in an election manifesto.
However, doing so would inevitably be politically difficult and, according to Professor Curtice, almost certain to be highly unpopular.
“The Brexit referendum in 2016 was not legally binding,” Sionaidh Douglas-Scott, the chair in Law at Queen Mary University of London, wrote by email. “Legally, it could have been ignored altogether. But it was thought to be politically unacceptable to ignore the public’s vote in the referendum. And political parties can ignore their election manifesto pledges at their peril,” she said, referring to parties’ reliance on public trust to support any agenda.
“I suspect Burnham might be tempted to have a referendum on the issue of rejoining the EU, feeling that public opinion had changed sufficiently to render a rejoin vote likely, although that’s by no means certain,” she said. “Some senior members of the [governing Labour] party … clearly feel that rejoining should be a manifesto pledge. So, politically, steps might be taken to make it more acceptable.”
Meanwhile, questions remained over the terms on which the UK might rejoin the bloc, whether it would be required to adopt the euro – a prospect it had previously resisted – and what form the EU itself might take following elections in some of its most influential member states, including France, Germany and Spain.
Polling suggests a distinction between support for closer relations with the EU as opposed to support for full membership.
While some surveys put support for rejoining at about 35 percent when closer ties were offered as an alternative, Curtice said support for closer relations was often less firmly held.
“Much of that support is soft – people say they somewhat support rather than strongly support” closer ties, he explained. By contrast, around half of those supporting rejoining the EU say they “strongly support” it, suggesting a deeper commitment to that option.
Similarly, at home, many of the more prominent figures of the original campaign to leave Europe have resurfaced and appear to be marshalling their forces against any return or realignment.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, one of Brexit’s most prominent campaigners, returned to Brussels on Thursday to oppose the prime minister’s efforts.
Other figures associated with the Leave campaign have also re-emerged, including former Prime Minister Boris Johnson and his former cabinet ally, Michael Gove, now a magazine editor. They have revived loosely sourced claims about the financial cost of rejoining the EU – or even of having remained a member. The campaign group Stay Out, for instance, puts the annual cost at 39.3 billion pounds (approximately $51.4bn), equivalent to 750 million pounds (about $982m) a week.
“I think we should think about two things when we think about Brexit and the potential to rejoin: trauma and salience,” Anand Menon, professor at King’s College London and director of UK in a Changing Europe, said. “Some people felt traumatised by the first debate and don’t want to revisit it. At the same time, the issue has lost its salience. The public don’t consider it one of the main issues facing the country,” he said.
“If you cast your mind back to 2016, those supporting Leave, like Nigel Farage, took the EU, which the public never really thought about, and linked it in the public’s mind to something they absolutely did: immigration.
“If Burnham is going to try to get the sort of energy he’ll need to see the process through, he’s going to need to do something similar, though what, I don’t know.”

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled a plan on Friday to shutter the notorious Rikers Island jail by the end of 2032, proposing to push the deadline from August 2027.
Rikers, long criticised for unsanitary conditions and violence, is due to be replaced by four borough-based jails as part of an effort to improve safety and tackle overcrowding.
The four new sites will be set in the Bronx, Brooklyn, Manhattan and Queens, with the Brooklyn facility scheduled to open in 2029.
The plan aims to bring facilities closer to courts, families and public transportation, while also reducing detention and case delay to help bring the jail population down from around 6,600 people to no more than 4,100 by the end of 2032.
“It is time to finally close Rikers Island,” Mamdani said in a statement released on Friday.
“For decades, New Yorkers have demanded a correctional system that is safe and humane," he continued. "This plan puts us on a path to deliver just that: closing Rikers, reducing pretrial detention, tackling the case delays that deprives people of their right to a speedy trial and investing $146 million in evidence-based supports that help break the cycles of incarceration."
"We have a legal and moral obligation to close Rikers," he added.
Rikers had been slated to close by August 2027 following legislation passed by the City Council in 2019. Moving the deadline will require a change to this law.
"Year after year, Rikers has taken a toll," Mamdani said in a press conference on Friday. "It has made us less safe. Because it has hollowed out those we love and failed those who need help. And because it has endured as a blight almost since the year it was built. A place we have long turned our eyes from rather than confront head on."
"Today, we lead differently. I am proud that New York City will close Rikers Island once and for all," he added.

“We don’t yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price…”
When the Steam Machine first started shipping in June , Valve said it was producing fewer units at a higher price than initially planned because it couldn’t secure supplies of scarce RAM and storage components at a reasonable cost. Now, as the last of the initial batch of Steam Machine reservations are finally being fulfilled, Valve says those supply and cost issues will continue into the foreseeable future and may even require a price change.
“We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units, but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels,” Valve wrote in a blog post on Thursday . “As a result we don’t yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we’ll be able to offer them. The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained.”
If Valve does have to raise the price of the Steam Machine, it will be in good company. All three major console manufacturers instituted historically atypical price increases in 2025 , with additional price hikes happening this year.
For the Steam Machine, though, Valve may be more susceptible to supply-related price shocks than its larger competitors in the gaming hardware space. Valve “likely [doesn’t] have the same kind of priority as a Nintendo, Sony, or Microsoft when it comes to suppliers,” F-Squared analyst Michael Futter told us earlier this year . And while the bigger players can still negotiate somewhat with chip suppliers, Valve’s Steam Machine is “a niche product that cannot benefit in the same way when it comes to procurement,” Niko Partners analyst Daniel Ahmad said.
While Valve has not publicly discussed total Steam Machine sales, estimates based on public Steam Top Sellers charts suggest the company was selling 12,000 to 15,000 a week back in July. By contrast, the PS5 has averaged over 300,000 weekly unit sales worldwide in its roughly six years on the market.
For now, at least, Valve says it has fulfilled an expectation it set in July that “everyone in the reservation queue will have the option to purchase by the end of this year.” The company now says there is “no waitlist remaining” for the 512GB Steam Machine model and that “purchase invites” have been sent to the remaining randomized 2TB reservation holders (who placed orders back in April). The 512GB model was even briefly back in stock on the Steam Store yesterday, even as Valve continues to pare down the waitlist for 2TB stock.
Valve says it plans to release additional updates on Steam Machine availability in January.

In a pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin, China's President Xi Jinping and President Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong province, on Thursday. Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Pool/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
President Trump is set to hold a White House press conference today at noon, following his return to Washington after a four-day trip to Asia , where he sat down for a rare three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump did not formally take questions while in China at the end of his trip, though it's typically expected on presidential foreign trips. Putin did hold a press conference before leaving the country.
The U.S. president said he will be discussing the historic meetings in China as well as trade agreements reached during the earlier part of the trip in the Philippines, where he arrived for the tail end of a summit with South Asian leaders.
Trump, Xi and Putin, who command the world's largest nuclear arsenals, gathered at a lakeside resort in Shenzhen, China, where they sat around a large round wooden table to discuss nuclear proliferation, Iran and global relations.
While the displays of power were prominent, the talks offered few signs that either Xi or Putin was prepared to make significant concessions to Trump.
"The trip enabled the president to bask in the glow of great power amity after a really bruising election outcome here at home," Suzanne Maloney, vice president and director of the foreign policy program at the Brookings Institution, said of Trump. "He wanted the optics of this direct engagement with Presidents Xi and Putin as a sort of validation of his own standing as a historical figure. And I think the photo op provided that."
Foreign trips are often largely about the pomp and circumstance involved in meetings between heads of state. Among other special events, Trump's arrival in China, for example, included a military flyover and young dancers.
But the events are also extensively choreographed, with aides working months in advance to lock down agreements and commitments that the leaders can point to as evidence of a successful trip. That did not appear to be a main objective for this visit.
For Xi, he was able to boast of China's global leadership by bringing together the world's greatest nuclear powers to discuss global challenges.
For Putin, the meeting allowed a chance to reestablish Russia as a great geopolitical power on par with China and the U.S.
And for Trump, it's a chance to turn the page and demonstrate his ongoing power at a time when he's been weakened domestically after the devastating midterm elections.
In his opening remarks alongside Xi and Putin, Trump said the three leaders were making history and that they had a responsibility to the rest of the world to maintain open and respectful dialogue.
"Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements. And we feel the opposite," Trump said. "No problems were ever solved under the old school, refusing to talk about it. No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech."
But while the kind words and pats on the back were prevalent, the lack of deliverables was also noteworthy.
It has raised questions about Trump's approach to foreign policy.
Trump has spent much of the last few years trying to replace the postwar rules-based order, ripping up traditional alliances in favor of a more personal approach to diplomacy. He prefers to work out deals personally with the world's superpowers.
But the visit may be demonstrating that access does not always produce results.
Xi and Putin have their own strategic objectives, which are not going to change because they're friendly with Trump. As Maloney put it, they also have to calculate whether agreements reached with Trump can survive domestic scrutiny or a change of administration in the coming years.
"I think both Putin and Xi recognized that President Trump's time is beginning to wane," Maloney said, "that his command of U.S. politics is also beginning to wane, and they're going to be looking to who and what may be coming next."

Bipartisan legislation now goes to the House amid concerns by some Democrats and environmental groups
The Senate approved bipartisan legislation on Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices.
The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure datacenters pay for the energy they use. Anger over datacenters and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.
The 62-33 vote is the first major action by Congress since midterm elections that soundly repudiated Donald Trump and congressional Republicans. The bill now goes to the House, which approved a more limited, industry-friendly version last year.
The Senate bill would overhaul several environmental laws to make it easier to build energy infrastructure, drawing criticism from Democrats and environmental groups about limits on judicial review and changes to bedrock laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act.
Trump urged approval of the bill, calling it a “BIG WIN for US ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” in a recent social media post. The bill, formally known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, will ensure the US can build pipelines, mines and power plants more quickly, “lowering Energy Costs for American Families”, Trump wrote.
Fifteen Democrats, including the Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, voted for the bill. Two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, voted no.
Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and the oil and gas sector support the bill as a way to deliver more electricity to the grid and avoid delays for infrastructure projects that can stretch a decade or more.
However, many environmental organizations have denounced the measure, saying it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.
“Make no mistake: this backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for datacenters, oil and gas pipelines and (liquefied natural gas) terminals while sacrificing fundamental and commonsense public health and environmental protections for communities across the US,” said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project.
Benefits for renewable energy are outweighed by likely increases in greenhouse gas emissions and air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry, Duggan and other critics said. She called the bill “a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America” and complained that it was being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without public hearings or sufficient debate.
A final vote on the measure was held up this week as Oregon’s two Democratic senators pushed to add amendments, including one to ban datacenters on public lands.
Senators Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden are among several Democrats in both chambers who say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that boosts clean energy, such as solar and wind power, while limiting expansion of oil, natural gas and other fossil fuels.
“Getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn’t tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels. Unfortunately, this bill does exactly that,” Merkley said.
Majority Republicans stymied Merkley’s effort to ensure votes on a host of amendments, including one that would block the Trump administration from continuing to cancel clean energy grants and other Democratic priorities for “purely political purposes”.
The bill’s sponsors reneged on promises of “a robust amendment process”, he said. In the end, the measure was approved without amendments offered by rank-and-file senators.
“I do think that this bill is very consequential to the future of this planet,” Merkley said.
Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, oppose the bill, citing concerns about limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws. The environmental policy law, known as Nepa, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved. The current review process often takes five years or more, and shortening that time frame is a key goal of the bill.
“In America today, it takes too long and costs too much to build,” said the Wyoming senator John Barrasso, the No 2 Republican in the Senate. “Energy projects that would help lower prices remain frozen for years” as they await approval by the federal government.
“Construction cannot start without first spending years in the regulatory penalty box,” driving up costs and creating uncertainty, Barrasso said.
The bill’s four main champions – two Democrats and two Republicans – have released a detailed set of amendments designed to bolster support for the legislation.
The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal a few weeks before the election. The Republican senators Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic senators Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.
“We are going to make it easier to build in America again, and make life more affordable for American families,” Lee said.
Whitehouse, a longtime climate hawk who has been criticized by some allies for supporting the permitting bill, said the measure was “the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations”, adding that he hoped “to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities” over the next two years.
But the Democratic senator Maria Cantwell of Washington state said the bill had been rushed and its impacts were not fully considered.
Cantwell, who met on Tuesday with tribal, outdoor recreation and conservation leaders, said the bill would undermine tribal nations and weaken protections for the nation’s bodies of water, land and wildlife.
“Now is the time to slow this process down, to actually have a formal process” to debate and amend the bill, she said. “Don’t sacrifice the Clean Water Act or hunting or fishing grounds, historic or sacred sites, or protections of tribal sovereignty. We all need new sources of energy and power. But this bill, as it’s currently drafted, is not the answer.”

Actor and author are alleged to have attacked and gang-raped a woman while filming together in 2018
French police are investigating allegations that the actor Gérard Depardieu and the author Michel Houellebecq gang-raped and assaulted a woman during a 2018 film shoot.
The alleged attack took place in December 2018 during the shooting of Thalasso, a film starring the two men as versions of themselves who meet at a health spa and have long philosophical conversations while in white bath-robes.
Two sources following the case confirmed to Agence France-Presse on Friday that a police investigation was under way.
The investigative website Mediapart reported this week that an actor, given the pseudonym Alexandra, had made a complaint to police in 2025.
Alexandra, an eastern European actor and dancer who was 32 at the time and working in France, told Mediapart that she was attacked by Depardieu and Houellebecq as they pinned her down during one scene and while cameras filmed.
Mediapart reported that Alexandra described being “in a state of stupefaction and disconnect”. In her police complaint she had spoken of “deep humiliation” and “indescribable shame”.
The film’s director, Guillaume Nicloux, had been accused of complicity in the sexual abuse, AFP reported.
Nicloux told Mediapart that at the moment of filming he had not “noticed any constraint”, but he had “apologised” to Alexandra.
Alexandra’s lawyers did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian. Depardieu’s lawyers did not respond to a request for comment. The Guardian contacted Houellebecq’s publishers, who did not respond.
This week Depardieu, 77, dropped his appeal against a 2025 conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a different film set in 2021, and apologised to them.
At his trial last year, Depardieu was found guilty of sexually assaulting a 55-year-old set dresser and a 35-year-old assistant director during the shooting of the feature film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters) in Paris in September 2021. His suspended sentence will now stand and his name has been added to France’s sex offender register.
After Depardieu’s apology this week, the assistant director whom he sexually assaulted said: “The monster of cinema has fallen.”
Depardieu’s conviction last year was a turning point for the #MeToo movement in France . He became the biggest figure in the French film industry to be convicted of sexual assault after years of criticism of the country’s reluctance to take women’s claims of abuse seriously.
He has appealed against a separate decision requiring him to face trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting the actor Charlotte Arnould at his Paris home in 2018. Appeal judges will rule this month on whether to uphold his appeal or allow the trial to go ahead next year.
In an open letter to Le Figaro in October 2023, Depardieu denied all allegations and said any encounter with Arnould had been consensual. “Never, ever, have I abused a woman,” he wrote.
Houellebecq, 70, who is among France’s most translated authors, is also under investigation for alleged incitement to discrimination in France over comments he made in 2022 about Muslims.
Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland , or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland . In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html
